sentence: Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) is a central nervous system stimulant used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a sleep disorder called narcolepsy.
Adderall contains a combination of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine, which affect chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control.
For ADHD, Adderall is used in children 3 to 17 years of age and in adults.
Adderall may help increase attention and decrease impulsiveness and hyperactivity.
For narcolepsy, Adderall is used in people 6 years and older.
It is not known if Adderall is safe and effective for ADHD in children under 3 years of age or for narcolepsy in children under 6 years of age.
Adderall is a federally controlled substance (CII) because Adderall contains amphetamine, which can be a target for people who abuse prescription medicines or street drugs.
Keep Adderall in a safe place to protect Adderall from theft.
Never give your Adderall to anyone else, because Adderall may cause death or harm them.
Selling or giving away Adderall is against the law.
Adderall may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide.
Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) was FDA-approved on January 19, 1960.
Extended-release formulations of Adderall (Adderall XR) are only used to treat ADHD.
Adderall has a Boxed Warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction.
Abuse, misuse, and addiction:
Adderall has a high chance of abuse and misuse and may lead to substance use problems, including addiction.
Misuse and abuse of Adderall, other amphetamine-containing medicines, and methylphenidate-containing medicines can lead to overdose and death.
The risk of overdose and death is increased with higher doses or when the medicine is used in ways that are not approved, such as snorting or injection.
Adderall may lead to physical dependence after prolonged use, even if taken as directed.
Your healthcare provider should check you or your child for the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction before starting treatment and will monitor you or your child during treatment.
Tell your healthcare provider if you or your child has ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines, or street drugs.
Heart-related risks:
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Your healthcare provider should check you or your child carefully for heart problems before starting Adderall and should check blood pressure and heart rate regularly during treatment.

Call your healthcare provider right away or go to the nearest hospital emergency room if you or your child have any signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting during treatment.
Mental (psychiatric) problems:

Adderall may cause new or worse behavior and thought problems, new or worse bipolar illness, or new psychotic symptoms (such as hearing voices, or seeing or believing things that are not real) or new manic symptoms.
This is more likely if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
Tell your healthcare provider about any mental problems you or your child have, or about a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression.

Call your healthcare provider right away if you or your child have any new or worsening mental symptoms during treatment, especially hearing voices, seeing or believing things that are not real, or new manic symptoms.
Circulation problems:
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained wounds appearing on your fingers or toes during treatment.
Other warnings:

Do not use Adderall if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine, or if you have received a methylene blue injection.
A dangerous drug interaction could occur.

You may not be able to use Adderall if you have glaucoma, an overactive thyroid, severe anxiety or agitation, moderate to severe high blood pressure, heart disease or coronary artery disease, vascular disease, or a history of drug or alcohol addiction.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to Adderall: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Serious side effects:
Adderall may cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, or feeling like you might pass out
signs of psychosis, such as hallucinations, new behavior problems, aggression, hostility, or paranoia
signs of circulation problems, such as numbness, pain, a cold feeling, unexplained wounds, or skin color changes (pale, red, or blue appearance) in your fingers or toes
a seizure
muscle twitches (tics)
changes in your vision.
See warnings above.
Slowing of growth (height and weight) in children:
Children should have their height and weight checked often during treatment, and your healthcare provider may stop treatment if your child is not growing or gaining weight as expected.
Serotonin syndrome:
This problem may happen when Adderall is taken with certain other medicines and may be life-threatening.

Stop taking Adderall and get medical help right away if you develop agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Common side effects:
Common side effects of Adderall may include stomach pain, loss of appetite, weight loss, mood changes, feeling nervous, fast heart rate, headache, dizziness, sleep problems (insomnia), and dry mouth.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Do not take Adderall if you or your child:
are allergic to amphetamine products or any of the ingredients in Adderall (see ingredients below)
are taking, or have taken within the past 14 days, an MAO inhibitor, including the antibiotic linezolid or the intravenous medicine methylene blue.
have a rare adrenal gland tumor called pheochromocytoma.
Before taking Adderall, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions including if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
heart problems, heart disease, heart defects, or high blood pressure, or a family history of sudden death or heart problems
mental problems including psychosis, mania, bipolar illness, or depression, or a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression
kidney or liver problems
seizures or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG)
circulation problems in the fingers or toes
repeated movements or sounds (tics) or Tourette's syndrome, or a family history of tics or Tourette's syndrome.
Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, intending to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
Taking Adderall during pregnancy can cause premature birth, low birth weight, or withdrawal symptoms in the newborn baby.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information about the health of females exposed to Adderall and females's babies.
Adderall passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby.
You should not breastfeed during treatment with Adderall.
Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed the baby during treatment.
Take Adderall exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
Follow all directions on your prescription label.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Do not take Adderall in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
The first dose of the day is usually taken when you first wake up.
Taking Adderall in the afternoon may cause trouble sleeping.
Adderall can be taken with or without food.
Do not crush or chew an extended-release capsule.
Swallow it whole.
To make swallowing easier, you may open the capsule and sprinkle Adderall into a spoonful of applesauce, then swallow all of the mixture right away without chewing.
Do not divide Adderall in the capsule, and do not save the mixture for later use.
Adderall may be habit-forming.
Never share Adderall with another person, especially someone with a history of drug abuse or addiction.
Keep Adderall where others cannot get to it.
While using Adderall, your doctor will need to check your progress at regular visits.
Adderall can cause unusual results with certain medical tests, so tell any doctor who treats you that you are using Adderall.
Your healthcare provider may tell you to stop taking Adderall for a short time before you get certain imaging tests.
Usual adult dose for ADHD:
Immediate-release (IR):
Initial dose: 5 mg orally 1 or 2 times a day.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Maximum dose: only in rare cases will Maximum dose be necessary to exceed 40 mg per day.
The first dose should be given upon awakening, with 1 to 2 additional doses at intervals of 4 to 6 hours.
Extended-release (XR), for patients starting treatment for the first time or switching from another medication:
Initial dose: 20 mg orally once a day.
Usual adult dose for narcolepsy:
Immediate-release (IR):
Initial dose: 10 mg orally per day in divided doses.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 10 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
The usual dose is 5 to 60 mg per day in divided doses, depending on the individual patient response.
The first dose should be given on awakening, with 1 to 2 additional doses at intervals of 4 to 6 hours.
Usual pediatric dose for ADHD:
Immediate-release (IR), ages 3 to 5 years:
Initial dose: 2.5 mg orally per day.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 2.5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Immediate-release (IR), ages 6 to 17 years:
Initial dose: 5 mg orally 1 or 2 times a day.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Maximum dose: only in rare cases will Maximum dose be necessary to exceed 40 mg per day.
Extended-release (XR), ages 6 to 12 years:
Initial dose: 5 or 10 mg orally once a day in the morning.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 to 10 mg increments at weekly intervals.
Maximum dose: 30 mg per day.
Extended-release (XR), ages 13 to 17 years:
Initial dose: 10 mg orally once a day.
Maintenance dose: may be increased to 20 mg per day after one week if symptoms are not adequately controlled.
Maximum dose: 30 mg per day.
Usual pediatric dose for narcolepsy:
Immediate-release (IR), ages 6 to 11 years:
Initial dose: 5 mg orally per day in divided doses.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Immediate-release (IR), ages 12 years and older:
Initial dose: 10 mg orally per day in divided doses.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 10 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Narcolepsy rarely occurs in children under 12 years of age.

An overdose of Adderall could be fatal.
Overdose symptoms may include restlessness, tremor, muscle twitches, rapid breathing, confusion, hallucinations, panic, aggressiveness, muscle pain or weakness, and dark colored urine.
These symptoms may be followed by depression and tiredness.
Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, uneven heartbeats, feeling light-headed, fainting, seizure, or coma.
Adderall may impair your thinking or reactions.
Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.
Avoid drinking fruit juices or taking vitamin C at the same time you take Adderall.
These can make your body absorb less of the medicine.

Q: How long does Adderall stay in your system (urine drug test)?
A: Adderall would take just over 2 days for a dose to be out of your system.
You should allow for longer (7 days) if you have taken Adderall frequently and at high doses.

Q: Adderall vs Vyvanse: Key Differences, Effectiveness, and Cost Comparison A: The primary difference between Adderall and Vyvanse lies in Adderall and Vyvanse's composition: Adderall contains a mixture of four different amphetamine salts, while Vyvanse contains only one type of amphetamine salt called lisdexamfetamine.
Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is a prodrug that converts into dexamphetamine once absorbed by the body.
Adderall's four amphetamine salts include dextroamphetamine saccharate, amphetamine aspartate, dextroamphetamine sulfate, and amphetamine sulfate.
Q: How should Adderall make you feel, with or without ADHD?
A: People taking Adderall for ADHD typically notice improved focus and attention and reduced impulsivity.
In people without ADHD, Adderall can also enhance focus, alertness, and energy levels.
Q: How long does Adderall last in your system?
A: When taken as prescribed, the effects of Adderall last for about 4 to 6 hours.
The effects of Adderall XR last for up to 12 hours because this brand of Adderall is designed for slow and sustained release.
Q: Modafinil (Provigil) vs Adderall: What's the difference?
A: Modafinil and Adderall are both classified as CNS stimulants but have different chemical structures, which means there are differences in their addiction potential and risk of side effects.
Modafinil and Adderall both have stimulant-type effects, but modafinil is a much milder stimulant than Adderall.
Q: Focalin vs Adderall: What's the difference?
A: Focalin contains dexmethylphenidate whereas Adderall contains a mixture of amphetamine salts (MAS).

Both have a high potential for abuse and dependence, although the risk may be perceived as higher with Adderall because Adderall is more popular; however, this does not mean Focalin is less likely to cause tolerance or dependence.
Q: How long does Adderall withdrawal last?
A: It is difficult to say exactly how long Adderall withdrawal lasts because Adderall withdrawal depends on the person and the process is different for everyone.
Some people’s withdrawal symptoms may resolve in as little as 5 days, others may still be experiencing symptoms 4 weeks later or even longer.
People who have taken Adderall for a long time at a high dose should expect withdrawal symptoms to last longer, sometimes several months.
Q: How do you get rid of Adderall tongue?
A: Adderall tongue is a common side effect of Adderall that can detrimentally and seriously affect a person’s quality of life.
To help relieve Adderall tongue stay well-hydrated.
Adderall and other ADHD medications can cause dehydration, so you need to drink at least 6 to 8 glasses of fluid per day.
Take frequent sips of water rather than drinking a whole glass of water at once.
Use artificial saliva products (such as sprays or lozenges) – artificial saliva products can help moisten the tissue and last longer than water.
There are many different brands of these available over the counter at drug stores and artificial saliva products can be used multiple times a day.
Chew sugar-free gum or suck on sugar-free candy – this contains xylitol which increases salivary flow and can help prevent dental decay.
Avoid sucking candy that contains sugar because sucking candy that contains sugar will increase your risk of dental decay
Q: Does Adderall help with anxiety and depression?

A: Although Adderall is only FDA-approved for the treatment of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy, Adderall has been used rarely and off-label to treat depression that has not responded to other treatments.
However, this is controversial and there is a lack of good quality evidence to support Adderall's use.
There is no evidence that Adderall helps with anxiety and in many people with pre-existing mood disorders, Adderall can make depression and/or anxiety worse.
Albuterol is a bronchodilator that relaxes muscles in the airways and increases air flow to the lungs.
Albuterol inhalation is used to treat or prevent bronchospasm, or narrowing of the airways in the lungs, in people with asthma or certain types of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Albuterol is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm.
Albuterol inhalation is for use in adults and children who are at least 2 years old.
Always follow your doctor's directions when giving albuterol to a child.
It is important to keep albuterol on hand at all times.
Get your prescription refilled before you run out of medicine completely.
Keep using all of your other medications as prescribed by your doctor.
Talk with your doctor if any of your asthma medications do not seem to work as well in treating or preventing attacks.
If albuterol seems like you need to use more of any of your medications in a 24-hour period, talk with your doctor.
An increased need for medication could be an early sign of a serious asthma attack.
Only use albuterol as prescribed by your physician.
An overdose of albuterol can be fatal.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
You should not use Albuterol if you are allergic to albuterol.
You should not use ProAir RespiClick or ProAir Digihaler if you are allergic to milk proteins.
To make sure albuterol inhalation is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have:
heart disease, high blood pressure, congestive heart failure;
a heart rhythm disorder;
a seizure disorder such as epilepsy;
diabetes;
overactive thyroid; or
low levels of potassium in your blood.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
It is not known whether albuterol will harm an unborn baby.

However, having uncontrolled asthma during pregnancy may increase the risk of premature birth, low birth weight, or eclampsia (dangerously high blood pressure that can lead to medical problems in both mother and baby).
The benefit of preventing bronchospasm may outweigh any risks to the baby.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of albuterol on the baby.
Pregnancy registry may not be safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.
Ask your doctor about any risk.

Q: Is Salbutamol the same as Albuterol?

A: Salbutamol and albuterol are the same active drug; “salbutamol” is the international generic name, while “albuterol” is the name used mainly in the United States for the same short‑acting beta‑2 agonist bronchodilator.
Salbutamol and albuterol share the same chemical structure, mechanism of action, and clinical uses.
Most differences patients notice relate to branding, country naming conventions, or inhaler devices, not the medicine itself.
Q: Can you use an expired albuterol inhaler?
A: An albuterol inhaler should be discarded after an expired albuterol inhaler passes an expired albuterol inhaler's expiration date.

Q: What is the best time of day to take blood pressure medication?

A: Research has suggested that taking your blood pressure medication at night instead of in the morning can provide better blood pressure control at night without compromising daytime blood pressure control and reduce your overall risk of dying because of cardiovascular disease by 45%.
Q: How long does it take for amlodipine to work?
A: Amlodipine decreases blood pressure over 4 to 8 hours after a single dose.
Because the decrease in blood pressure is gradual, a patient's heart rate is not affected because their physiological reflexes (such as an increase in heart rate) are not activated.
Q: How do I reduce swelling from amlodipine?
A: Swelling from amlodipine is a common, but often troublesome side effect of amlodipine with 5% to 9% of people stopping amlodipine because of it.
If you develop swelling with amlodipine, tell your doctor right away because doctor may be able to change your blood pressure medications slightly to help reduce the swelling.

Swelling caused by amlodipine does not usually respond to treatment with diuretics (such as furosemide) because Swelling is caused by changes in capillary pressure that result in leakage into the spaces between capillaries (called the interstitial area) rather than water retention.
Q: Best time to take amlodipine - day or night?
A: You can take amlodipine in the morning or at night, whichever works best for your schedule.
The key is to take amlodipine at the same time each day to maintain consistent blood levels and support amlodipine's effectiveness.
Q: How long does amlodipine stay in your system?
A: Amlodipine can stay in your system for up to 11.5 days after your last dose.

The risk of edema is greater in women compared with men and in those people taking a higher dosage of amlodipine, and edema is usually noticed as weight gain.

Q: Xarelto vs Eliquis: How do Xarelto vs Eliquis compare?
A: Xarelto (rivaroxaban) and Eliquis (apixaban) are novel anticoagulants that make blood less likely to clot (also called thinning the blood).
Both belong to the class of medicines known as factor Xa (FXa) inhibitors and they are two of the most popular blood thinners on the market.
Either one may be used to reduce the risk of stroke or treat and prevent blood clots in conditions such as DVT.
Q: What medications are known to cause hair loss?
A: Medication-induced hair loss represents a significant concern for patients across multiple therapeutic categories.

While chemotherapy drugs are most commonly associated with severe hair loss, many commonly prescribed medications-including antibiotics, psychiatric drugs, cardiovascular agents, and hormonal therapies-can also cause this distressing side effect.
Q: How do you reverse bleeding with Xarelto?

Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.
Atorvastatin works by selectively blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme the liver uses to produce cholesterol.

By slowing this process, Atorvastatin reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.
As a result, Atorvastatin lowers overall LDL levels, decreases the number of LDL particles, and improves the body’s ability to clear cholesterol.
Atorvastatin FDA-approved uses:
To reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in adults with:
Multiple risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD), but without established CHD.
Use: to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina.
Type 2 diabetes and multiple risk factors for CHD, without established CHD Use: to help reduce the risk of MI and stroke.
Adults with clinically evident CHD: Use: To reduce the risk of non-fatal MI, fatal and non-fatal stroke, revascularization procedures, hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and angina.
As an adjunct to diet to lower LDL-C:
Adults with primary hyperlipidemia.
Adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).
As an adjunct to other LDL-lowering therapies:
For adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
As an adjunct to diet for additional lipid disorders in adults:
Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia.
Hypertriglyceridemia.

Q: Best time to take atorvastatin: Morning or Night?
A: Atorvastatin can generally be taken either in the morning or at night, because Atorvastatin is a long‑acting statin that stays active in the body around the clock.
The most important factor is taking Atorvastatin at the same time every day so your cholesterol levels and cardiovascular protection remain stable over time.
Q: Rosuvastatin or Atorvastatin: What’s the better choice for you?
A: Rosuvastatin (Crestor) and atorvastatin (Lipitor) are both statins that lower “bad” LDL cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at increased cardiovascular risk.
The better choice for you depends on factors such as how much LDL reduction you need, your medical history, and cost and insurance coverage.
Q: Do I need to eat food when taking atorvastatin?
A: Atorvastatin (also known as Lipitor) can be taken any time of the day, with or without food.
An oral dose of atorvastatin will be absorbed rapidly, with maximum plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours after you take atorvastatin.
While you may or may not eat food when taking atorvastatin, there are certain foods you should avoid when taking the drug.
Q: How long does atorvastatin stay in the system after stopping atorvastatin?
A: Atorvastatin takes about 77 hours (3 days) for atorvastatin to be out of your system.
The elimination half life of atorvastatin is approximately 14 hours.
This is the time atorvastatin takes for your body to reduce plasma drug levels by half.
Atorvastatin takes approximately 5.5 x elimination half lives for a medicine to be out of ones system.
Q: Does atorvastatin cause weight gain?

A: Atorvastatin Atorvastatin does not consistently cause weight gain in clinical trials, but some studies suggest a small association between statin use (including atorvastatin) and modest weight gain and higher diabetes risk over time.
For most people, the heart‑protective benefits of atorvastatin outweigh these potential metabolic effects, especially when combined with lifestyle measures that support a healthy weight.

There just hasn't been as much research published regarding how other types of citrus (apart from grapefruit) interact with statins.
Large quantities of lime or lime peel should be avoided, although small amounts (such as a twist of lime in a drink) are unlikely to cause a significant interaction.

Q: Can you take Benadryl and cetirizine together?
A: Benadryl should not be taken at the same time as cetirizine because cetirizine can increase side effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, and difficulty concentrating.
Some people, especially the elderly or children, may also find their thinking, judgement, and coordination impaired.
You should also not drink alcohol while taking either of Benadryl because it can make these side effects worse.
Q: Can cetirizine raise blood pressure?
A: Cetirizine does not increase blood pressure and blood pressure is not listed as a side effect in the product information.
But cetirizine can be found in combination with other medications, such as pseudoephedrine in products such as Zyrtec-D, and pseudoephedrine does increase blood pressure.
Q: Is cetirizine OK to take antihistamines every day?
A: Yes, most people can take antihistamines every day, if people have daily symptoms of people's allergies.
If you have chronic allergies with daily symptoms, you may take a daily antihistamine.
Q: Should cetirizine be taken at bedtime or upon awakening?
A: Cetirizine can be taken at any time of day.
Most people do not feel drowsy when taking cetirizine, so they often take cetirizine in the morning.
However, a small number of people do experience sedation.
If cetirizine makes you feel drowsy, it is best to take cetirizine in the evening.
Q: Which antihistamines make you drowsy?
A: First-generation antihistamines, like Benadryl (diphenhydramine) and Chlor-Trimeton (chlorpheniramine), often cause sedation.
First-generation antihistamines can include drowsiness, fatigue, and reduced alertness or concentration.
Q: Can you take antihistamines when pregnant?
A: According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), several over-the-counter (OTC) antihistamines may be taken during pregnancy.
Older, first-generation antihistamines can be taken, but antihistamines may cause drowsiness.
Newer, second-generation antihistamines can also be taken and have less risk of drowsiness.
Q: How long does it take for cetirizine to work?
A: Cetirizine is an allergy medicine that usually starts to work within about 20 to 60 minutes after you take it.
Many people notice less sneezing and itching within the first hour, especially if they take cetirizine on an empty stomach.
One dose of cetirizine generally provides relief for up to 24 hours, so most people only need to take cetirizine once a day.
Q: Does cetirizine make you drowsy?
A: Cetirizine is considered a non-drowsy (second-generation) antihistamine, but Cetirizine can still cause drowsiness in some people.
In clinical studies, the chance of feeling sleepy increased with higher doses.
Q: How long after taking cetirizine can I drink alcohol?
A: It is best to wait until cetirizine completely leaves your body before you drink alcohol, which may take up to 40 hours (almost 2 days).

Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant used short-term to relieve muscle spasms caused by sprains, strains, and injuries, including low back and neck pain.
Cyclobenzaprine is used together with rest and physical therapy to help relieve the pain, tenderness, and limited movement caused by muscle spasm.
Cyclobenzaprine is also used to treat fibromyalgia in adults, where Cyclobenzaprine can help reduce pain.
For fibromyalgia, Cyclobenzaprine is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya.
In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks, and close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain.
The Flexeril brand has been discontinued, but cyclobenzaprine is available as generic tablets and as the brand-name products Amrix (extended-release capsules) and Fexmid.
Cyclobenzaprine works by reducing the nerve signals in the brain that drive muscle tone and spasm, which allows tight, overactive muscles to relax.
Cyclobenzaprine acts within the central nervous system, primarily at the level of the brain stem, and does not act on the muscles themselves or at the junction between nerves and muscle.

1,2 Because cyclobenzaprine works through the nervous system in this way, Cyclobenzaprine will not relieve muscle spasm caused by central nervous system disease, such as cerebral palsy or spinal cord disease.
The way cyclobenzaprine works in fibromyalgia is not known.
Laboratory studies show Cyclobenzaprine blocks several receptor types, including serotonin (5-HT2A), histamine, and muscarinic receptors.

Cyclobenzaprine is chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which explains several of Cyclobenzaprine's side effects (such as drowsiness and dry mouth) and some of Cyclobenzaprine's most important drug interactions.

Dangerously high fever, seizures, and deaths have occurred when cyclobenzaprine or similar drugs were combined with these medicines.

Cyclobenzaprine can cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome when taken with certain other medicines, especially antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics), tramadol, bupropion, meperidine, and verapamil.
Get medical help right away if you have agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Drowsiness and alcohol.
Cyclobenzaprine can impair your thinking and reactions, and this effect is stronger with alcohol or other medicines that cause drowsiness.
Do not drive or do anything that needs alertness until you know how it affects you.
Pregnancy: If you use Tonmya for fibromyalgia.
Based on animal studies, Tonmya may increase the risk of neural tube defects (a type of birth defect affecting the spine) if used in early pregnancy.
Do not use Tonmya in the two weeks before conception or during the first trimester.
See the Pregnancy section below.

hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid);
heart block, a heart rhythm disorder, or congestive heart failure; or
had a recent heart attack.
To make sure cyclobenzaprine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
liver disease; 1,2,3
glaucoma or increased pressure in the eye; 1,2,3
a seizure disorder (Tonmya); 3
an enlarged prostate or problems with urination.
The safety and effectiveness of cyclobenzaprine tablets have not been established in children under 15 years of age.
The safety and effectiveness of Tonmya and Amrix have not been established in children of any age.
Older adults:
Cyclobenzaprine builds up to higher levels in older adults and is more likely to cause side effects such as confusion, hallucinations, heart problems, and falls.
In people 65 and older:
Immediate-release tablets should be used only if clearly needed, starting at 5 mg and increasing slowly under medical supervision.

Amrix extended-release capsules are not recommended at all, because blood levels run about 40% higher and Amrix stays in the body much longer (half-life of 50 hours versus 32 hours in younger adults).
Tonmya is limited to the lower 2.8 mg dose once daily at bedtime.
Pregnancy:
Pregnancy guidance differs by product, so check which cyclobenzaprine product you use.
Tonmya (fibromyalgia): Based on animal data, Tonmya may increase the risk of neural tube defects when used two weeks before conception and through the first trimester.
Because neural tube development happens early, often before pregnancy is recognized, avoid Tonmya during this window.
Your healthcare provider should do a pregnancy test before you start Tonmya, and you should use effective contraception during treatment and for two weeks after the final dose.

Immediate-release tablets and Amrix (muscle spasm): available data have not identified a risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, and animal studies at usual doses did not show harm to the fetus, although data are limited.
Cyclobenzaprine should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Breastfeeding:
Small published reports suggest cyclobenzaprine passes into breast milk in low amounts, but there is no information on effects on a breastfed baby or on milk supply.
Talk with your healthcare provider about the benefits of breastfeeding alongside your need for Cyclobenzaprine.
Cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm:
Cyclobenzaprine is usually taken for up to 2 or 3 weeks for muscle spasm.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day.
Extended-release capsules are taken once daily, at about the same time each day.

Swallow the capsules whole; if you have difficulty swallowing them, you can open the capsule and sprinkle the contents onto a tablespoon of applesauce, then swallow the mixture right away without chewing.
Follow your doctor's dosing instructions very carefully.
Cyclobenzaprine for fibromyalgia:
Tonmya is taken once daily at bedtime, after brushing your teeth.
Drink a few sips of water first so your mouth is moist, place the tablet(s) under your tongue until dissolved, and do not swallow whole, cut, crush, or chew.
Avoid eating or drinking for at least 15 minutes afterward, avoid hot, cold, or acidic drinks until morning, and avoid talking for about 5 minutes after dosing.
The usual cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm is 5 mg three times a day, which may be increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed.
The maximum dose is 30 mg per day.
Cyclobenzaprine is taken for a maximum of 2 to 3 weeks.
Cyclobenzaprine dosage chart:
Immediate-release tablets: the usual starting dose is 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day based on your response.
In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver problems, treatment should start at 5 mg and be increased slowly, if at all.
The tablets are not recommended with moderate to severe liver impairment.
Amrix extended-release capsules: the recommended dose is 15 mg once daily for most adults; some people may need 30 mg once daily (one 30 mg capsule or two 15 mg capsules).
Amrix is not recommended in adults 65 and older, or in anyone with liver impairment of any severity.

Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia): The recommended starting dose of Tonmya is 2.8 mg (1 sublingual tablet) once daily at bedtime for the first 14 days, then increases to the target dose of 5.6 mg (2 sublingual tablets) once daily at bedtime from day 15 onward.
The maximum is 5.6 mg once daily.
In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver impairment, the maximum is 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime, and Tonmya is not recommended with moderate or severe liver impairment.
Product | Usual adult dose | Maximum dose | How long

Immediate-release tablets, formerly sold as Flexeril (adults and children 15 and older) | 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed | 30 mg per day (10 mg three times a day) | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Amrix extended-release capsules | 15 mg once daily | 30 mg once daily | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia) | 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime for 14 days, then 5.6 mg once daily at bedtime | 5.6 mg once daily | Ongoing, as directed
Can I take 2 cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at the same time?
No.
Do not take two cyclobenzaprine 10 mg tablets at once.
The maximum recommended single dose of the immediate-release tablet is 10 mg, taken up to three times a day.

Taking 20 mg at one time increases the risk of side effects such as severe drowsiness and fast heart rate, and in overdose cyclobenzaprine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, without providing better muscle spasm relief.
If your dose is not controlling your symptoms, talk with your doctor rather than doubling up.
How often can you take cyclobenzaprine?
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day.
Amrix extended-release capsules and Tonmya sublingual tablets are taken once a day.
Do not take extra doses between scheduled doses.
How long does cyclobenzaprine take to work, and how long does cyclobenzaprine last?

In clinical trials of the immediate-release tablets, the muscle relaxant effect was measurable within the first several days, with significant improvement in muscle spasm and pain by day 3 or 4 of treatment.
With Amrix extended-release capsules, Cyclobenzaprine is first detectable in the blood about 1.5 hours after a dose, with peak levels at 7 to 8 hours, and one daily dose provides day-long coverage.
How long does cyclobenzaprine stay in your system?
Cyclobenzaprine stays in your system for about 3 to 7 days after your last dose.
Cyclobenzaprine has a half-life of around 18 hours for the immediate-release tablets, and a drug takes 4 to 5 half-lives to clear from the body.

The once-daily forms last longer: the half-life is about 32 hours for Amrix extended-release capsules and about 36 hours for Tonmya sublingual tablets, so Amrix extended-release capsules can take a week or more to fully clear.
Cyclobenzaprine also stays in the body longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, in whom blood levels run higher.
Does cyclobenzaprine show up on a drug test?

No, cyclobenzaprine does not usually show up on a drug test, as cyclobenzaprine is not a controlled substance and cyclobenzaprine is not one of the five substances (amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine) required on standard federal workplace drug tests.

However, cyclobenzaprine has a similar structure to tricyclic antidepressants, and Cyclobenzaprine is a recognized cause of false positive results on tricyclic antidepressant immunoassays, including urine immunoassays.
Tests for tricyclic antidepressants are not part of routine drugs-of-abuse screening.
If you take cyclobenzaprine and need a drug test, tell the testing provider what medicines you take.
A screening result is only presumptive, and a confirmatory laboratory test such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry can tell cyclobenzaprine apart from a tricyclic antidepressant.

An overdose of cyclobenzaprine can be fatal, and deliberate overdoses often involve other drugs or alcohol, which raises the danger.
Overdose symptoms may include severe drowsiness, fast heartbeats, tremors, agitation, slurred speech, confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, or hallucinations.
Rare but critical effects include seizures, dangerously low blood pressure, heart rhythm disturbances, and cardiac arrest.
Avoid driving or hazardous activity until you know how cyclobenzaprine will affect you.
Cyclobenzaprine can impair your thinking and reactions, and this effect is stronger with alcohol or other medicines that cause drowsiness.
Avoid drinking alcohol while taking cyclobenzaprine.
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache.
Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome.
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
drowsiness and tiredness;
dry mouth;
dizziness;
fatigue;
headache;
nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
blurred vision;
unpleasant taste;
nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness.

With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth.
Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour.
Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness.
Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe.
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching.
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults.
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials.
This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since 5 mg causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness.
Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for cyclobenzaprine to work.
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials.
Constipation results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

The most serious cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) drug interactions are with MAO inhibitors, which must never be combined with cyclobenzaprine, and with antidepressants and other serotonergic medicines, which can cause serotonin syndrome.
Cyclobenzaprine also interacts with alcohol and other medicines that cause drowsiness, making sedation worse.
Other medicines and substances that interact with cyclobenzaprine include: 1,2,3
MAO inhibitors such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, and tranylcypromine (contraindicated; do not use within 14 days);
antidepressants of any kind, including SSRIs, SNRIs, and tricyclics (risk of serotonin syndrome);
bupropion, tramadol, or meperidine;
verapamil;
alcohol;
opioid medicines, sleeping pills, other muscle relaxers, and medicines for anxiety or seizures;
barbiturates and other CNS depressants;
anticholinergic medicines;
guanethidine or similar blood pressure medicines;
cold or allergy medicines containing an antihistamine.
Cyclobenzaprine may increase the risk of seizures in people taking tramadol, and may block the blood pressure-lowering effect of guanethidine and similar drugs.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines.
This list is not complete, and other drugs may interact with cyclobenzaprine, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Can you take ibuprofen with cyclobenzaprine?

There is no listed drug interaction between cyclobenzaprine and ibuprofen, and the two are commonly prescribed together for painful muscle injuries, since cyclobenzaprine and ibuprofen work in different ways.

In studies, taking cyclobenzaprine with aspirin did not change blood levels of either drug, and combining cyclobenzaprine with naproxen was well tolerated, although the combination caused more drowsiness than naproxen alone.
Check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining medicines, especially if you take other drugs as well.
Can you take Tylenol with cyclobenzaprine?
There is no listed interaction between cyclobenzaprine and acetaminophen (Tylenol), and cyclobenzaprine and acetaminophen may be used together when recommended by your doctor.
Be careful with combination cold or nighttime products, which may contain antihistamines or other sedating ingredients that do interact with cyclobenzaprine.
Flexeril was the original brand name for cyclobenzaprine and remains the name many people know Flexeril by.

The Flexeril brand has been discontinued and is no longer on the marke t, but Flexeril was a commercial decision, not a safety withdrawal: generic cyclobenzaprine tablets containing the same active ingredient remain widely available and inexpensive.
Current brand names include Amrix (15 mg and 30 mg extended-release capsules taken once daily), Fexmid (7.5 mg tablets), and Tonmya (2.8 mg sublingual tablets for fibromyalgia, approved August 2025).
Q: Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?
A: Yes, cyclobenzaprine can make you very sleepy and this side effect may get worse with higher doses.
Drowsiness is the most commonly reported side effect in studies, occurring in up to 38% (38 out of 100) of people.
Fatigue and dizziness may also occur.
Avoid or limit the use of alcohol or other sedating medicines while being treated with cyclobenzaprine.
Also avoid driving, operating machinery, or other hazardous activities until you know how cyclobenzaprine affects you.

Q: What helps with Cymbalta withdrawal symptoms?
A: The best way to help with Cymbalta (duloxetine) withdrawal is to stop the medicine slowly, over 2 to 4 weeks or longer, with your prescriber’s help.
A slow, step-down plan (called a taper) gives your brain time to adjust and lowers the chance of symptoms like dizziness, nausea, and headache.

Q: Does Cymbalta cause weight gain?

Q: How to sleep while taking Cymbalta?
A: Not being able to sleep (also called insomnia) is one of the most common side effects reported by people taking Cymbalta.
In some people, this side effect improves after a couple of weeks of taking Cymbalta, but difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep can persist in others.
Here are some ways you can improve sleep while taking Cymbalta: Take your dose of Cymbalta in the morning.

Cymbalta may be given once a day or twice a day but for those people experiencing insomnia, Cymbalta should be taken just once a day in the morning Swallow Cymbalta capsules whole; do not crush, chew, or open up the capsules and sprinkle them on food because this may cause Cymbalta to be absorbed more quickly than intended, increasing the risk of side effects such as insomnia...

Symptoms such as depressed mood and lack of interest in activities may take the full 6-8 weeks to resolve.
When Cymbalta is used for pain, Cymbalta generally improves within two weeks.

Most report feeling these in the brain although some report them in other parts of the body.
They have been described as feeling like a short, low voltage, electric shock.

Q: Why does Lexapro (escitalopram) cause weight gain?

Complete Patient Guide A: Lexapro weight gain affects up 25 % to 41% of patients who take this antidepressant medication, although weight gain tends to be minimal, with an average gain of approximately 1 % to 3.7%.
The weight gain associated with Lexapro occurs primarily due to the drug's mechanism of action on serotonin levels in the brain.

When Lexapro blocks the serotonin transporter, Lexapro successfully increases serotonin availability to help treat depression and anxiety, but this same action can trigger unwanted changes in appetite and metabolism.

Q: How long does it take for Lexapro (escitalopram) to work?

Q: How long does it take for famotidine to work?
A: Famotidine starts to block stomach acid within 15 minutes to 1 hour of taking the medicine.
The maximum effect usually occurs within 1 to 3 hours, and lasts for 10 to 12 hours after a single dose.
Famotidine will also work to prevent heartburn if taken 10 to 60 minutes before a meal.
Do not take more than 2 tablets in 24 hours.
Q: Is famotidine better to take famotidine in the morning or at night?
A: In general, you can take over-the-counter (OTC) famotidine (Pepcid AC, Zantac 360) at any time of the day or night to help treat heartburn symptoms.
Studies have shown it is best to take OTC famotidine 1 hour before an evening meal to help prevent heartburn and indigestion in the evening and during bedtime which may interfere with your sleep.
Talk to your healthcare provider if your symptoms are severe or ongoing after 14 days.
Q: How much famotidine can I take in one day?
A: The maximum daily dose of over-the-counter (OTC) famotidine (Pepcid AC, Zantac 360) in adults and children over 12 years of age is 40 mg per day unless your doctor prescribes famotidine otherwise.
If your symptoms persist more than 2 weeks, contact your doctor.
Higher doses may be used for other conditions such as erosive esophagitis or Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome.
Q: Is famotidine safer than omeprazole for heartburn?

A: For most people with mild, occasional heartburn, famotidine is usually the safer first choice because famotidine works quickly, can be taken as needed, and has fewer long‑term safety concerns than omeprazole.

Omeprazole, a stronger acid reducer, may be a better option if you have frequent heartburn two or more days per week or confirmed GERD, but Omeprazole is linked with more potential risks when used for many months or at high doses.
Q: Can you take famotidine long term?

A: Yes, you could take omeprazole in the morning and famotidine at night but there are not many studies investigating this approach.
Preliminary results suggest that taking your medication this way may provide superior control of gastric acid secretion at night without compromising the effectiveness of omeprazole in the morning.
More research is needed.

Q: What are the risks of using Flonase long-term?
A: Using Flonase (fluticasone) longer than the label recommends can raise your risk of nosebleeds, nose sores, and a yeast infection in your nose or throat.
Rarer, body-wide risks include glaucoma or cataracts, bone loss, adrenal gland problems, and slower growth in children.

Q: How often can you use Flonase nasal spray?

A: Flonase (fluticasone propionate) nasal spray is used once per day in both adults and children to provide 24-hour relief from allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny nose, nasal congestion, and itchy, watery eyes.
Nasal steroids like Flonase are most effective when used on a regular basis.
Flonase may take 3 to 4 days of regular use for the full effect during allergy season.
Q: Which is stronger, Flonase OTC or prescription?
A: Over-the-counter (OTC) Flonase Allergy Relief is exactly the same strength, dose and medicine as prescription Flonase.

The brand-name prescription Flonase has been discontinued in the U.S., but OTC Flonase, generic fluticasone, and store brands are still sold.
Q: How long does it take for Flonase to work?
A: While many people feel effects after the first dose, Flonase may take 3 to 4 days of regular use of Flonase nasal spray for the full effect on allergy symptoms.
For this reason, nasal steroids like Flonase are most effective when used on a regular basis for long-term relief.

Fluoxetine is a prescription antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), bulimia nervosa, and panic disorder.
When used together with olanzapine (Zyprexa), Fluoxetine is also used to treat depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder and treatment-resistant depression.
Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
The original brand name of fluoxetine is Prozac, and it's now available as a generic.
Fluoxetine is FDA-approved to treat the following conditions:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 8 years and older
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 7 years and older
Bulimia nervosa for acute and maintenance treatment of binge-eating and purging in adults with moderate to severe bulimia
Panic disorder for the treatment of panic attacks in adults
When used in combination with olanzapine, fluoxetine is also FDA-approved for:
Acute treatment of depressive episodes associated with Bipolar I disorder (depressive episodes) in adults and children aged 10 years and older
Treatment-resistant depression for adults who have not responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials
Fluoxetine alone is not approved for bipolar I depressive episodes or treatment-resistant depression - olanzapine must be used in combination for these indications.
Fluoxetine works by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, leaving more of serotonin active between nerve cells.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep.
By increasing the availability of serotonin, fluoxetine can relieve symptoms of depression, anxiety, and OCD.
Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
SSRIs are one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressant classes because SSRIs are generally well-tolerated and effective across a range of conditions.
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.
Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects.
Not everyone experiences side effects, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication.

Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment.
Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior.

Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed.
This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting Fluoxetine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels.
This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications.
Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking Fluoxetine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
Abnormal bleeding: Fluoxetine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): Fluoxetine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people.
An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss.
Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults.
Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat.
Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function.
In men, Sexual dysfunction may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems.
In women, Sexual dysfunction may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm.
Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
Drowsiness and impaired concentration: Fluoxetine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly.
Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how Fluoxetine affects you.
Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking Fluoxetine.
Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking Fluoxetine, and high blood sugar when Fluoxetine is stopped.
Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.
Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and medications before starting fluoxetine (Prozac), as some may interact with fluoxetine or affect whether it is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
Triptans (for migraine)
Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
Amphetamines
Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome, a potentially serious condition.
Tell your doctor if you have or have had any of the following:
Liver, kidney, or heart problems
Seizures or epilepsy
Bipolar disorder or mania
Low sodium levels in the blood
A stroke or high blood pressure
Bleeding problems
Pregnancy
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, become pregnant, or plan to become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets.

Using fluoxetine later in pregnancy may increase the risk of complications in the newborn, including problems that need a longer hospital stay, breathing support, or tube feeding, and a serious lung condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).
Untreated depression also carries risks in pregnancy, so discuss the benefits and risks of treatment with your healthcare provider rather than stopping on your own.

If you become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets, ask your healthcare provider about joining the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants, which tracks pregnancy outcomes in women who take these medicines.
You can enroll by calling 1-866-961-2388 or visiting womensmentalhealth.org.
Breastfeeding:
Fluoxetine passes into breast milk.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed, and discuss the best way to feed your baby while you are taking fluoxetine tablets.
If you do breastfeed, watch your baby for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, or poor weight gain, and seek medical advice if you notice any of these.
Take fluoxetine exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Swallow the delayed-release capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
Measure liquid medicine carefully.
Use the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
It may take up to 4 weeks before your symptoms improve.
Keep using the medication as directed and tell your doctor if your symptoms do not improve.
Tell your doctor if you have any changes in sexual function, such as loss of interest in sex, trouble having an orgasm, or (in men) problems with erections or ejaculation.
Some sexual problems can be treated.
Do not stop using fluoxetine suddenly, or you could have unpleasant withdrawal symptoms.
Ask your doctor how to safely stop using fluoxetine.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.
Fluoxetine (Prozac) is taken orally, and your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition, age, and response to treatment.
Always follow your doctor's instructions, do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine without speaking to doctor first.
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD):
Adults: Treatment typically starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning.
Your doctor may increase the dose after several weeks if needed.
The maximum dose is 80 mg/day.
Children and adolescents (aged 8 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg or 20 mg per day.
In lower-weight children, the starting dose and target dose may remain at 10 mg/day.
With all patients, the full effect of fluoxetine for depression may take 4 weeks or longer.
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD):
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning and may be increased after several weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement.
The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day.
Full therapeutic effect may take 5 weeks or longer.
Adolescents and higher-weight children (aged 7 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after 2 weeks.
Additional dose increases may be considered after several more weeks if insufficient clinical improvement is observed.
The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day.
Lower-weight children: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day with dose increases after several more weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement.
The recommended dose range of 20 mg to 30 mg per day, although experience with daily doses greater than 20 mg is very minimal,
Bulimia Nervosa:
Adult dose: The recommended dose is 60 mg once daily in the morning.
Your doctor may gradually increase your dose to this level over several days.
Clinical trials showed that the 60 mg dose was effective in reducing binge-eating and purging behaviors.
Panic Disorder:
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after one week.
Your doctor may adjust the dose after several weeks if needed.
Clinical trials used a dose range of 10 mg/day to 60 mg/day, but the most commonly used dose in clinical trials was 20 mg/day.
General Dosing Notes:
Fluoxetine is usually taken in the morning to minimize the risk of sleep disturbances
It may take several weeks to feel the full benefit of fluoxetine, do not stop taking fluoxetine without talking to your doctor first
Your doctor will periodically reassess whether you need to continue treatment
Older adults may need a lower dose or may take fluoxetine less frequently than younger adults
People with liver problems may also require a lower or less frequent dose
If you have other medical conditions or take multiple medications, your doctor may need to adjust your fluoxetine dose accordingly
