Is 40mg of fluoxetine a high dose?
40mg of fluoxetine is considered a moderate maintenance dose in adults for major depressive disorder (MDD) and OCD.
The standard starting dose for most conditions is 20mg per day, except for panic disorder, which starts at 10mg.
If symptoms have not improved after several weeks, the dose may be increased, up to 40mg for MDD and OCD, or 20mg for panic disorder.
The recommended dose for bulimia is 60mg per day.
Your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition and response to treatment.
Does fluoxetine cause weight gain?
Fluoxetine is less likely to cause weight gain than many other antidepressants.
In the short term, Fluoxetine can actually cause mild weight loss due to reduced appetite, which is one of Fluoxetine's common side effects.
However, some people do experience weight changes over longer-term use.
If you notice significant weight changes while taking Fluoxetine, speak to your doctor, as dose adjustments or alternative treatments may be available.
How long does fluoxetine take to work?
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.
Some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy levels may be noticeable within the first 1 to 2 weeks, but mood and motivation typically take longer to improve.
For obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) may take 5 weeks or longer to see the full benefit.
It is important to keep taking fluoxetine as prescribed, even if you do not feel immediate improvement.
Do not stop without speaking to your doctor first.
Is fluoxetine a controlled substance?
No, fluoxetine is not a controlled substance.
It is not classified under the DEA Controlled Substances Act, meaning fluoxetine does not have recognized potential for dependence or abuse in the way that drugs like opioids or benzodiazepines do.
Fluoxetine is, however, a prescription-only medicine, so fluoxetine still requires a valid prescription from a licensed healthcare provider.
Is fluoxetine an SSRI?
Yes, fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI).
SSRIs work by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, increasing the amount of serotonin available between nerve cells.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep.
Prozac was one of the first SSRIs approved and remains one of the most widely prescribed antidepressants worldwide.
What are the side effects of fluoxetine in females?
Females may experience all of the common fluoxetine side effects, but some side effects are particularly relevant to women:
Sexual side effects are common, including decreased sex drive (libido) and difficulty reaching orgasm.
Sexual side effects can affect quality of life and should be discussed with your doctor, as treatment options are available.
Weight changes - Fluoxetine may cause mild weight loss initially, though longer-term weight changes can occur.
Menstrual changes - some women report changes to their menstrual cycle, though Menstrual changes is not among the most commonly reported side effects.
Pregnancy - taking Fluoxetine in late pregnancy may increase the risk of certain complications in newborns.
Women who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding should discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor before continuing or starting this medicine.
Does fluoxetine (Prozac) help with anxiety?
Fluoxetine is not FDA-approved specifically for generalized anxiety disorder, but Fluoxetine is FDA-approved to treat panic disorder, which is a type of anxiety disorder.
Fluoxetine is also approved for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which has a significant anxiety component.

Although not FDA-approved for generalized anxiety disorder, Fluoxetine is sometimes prescribed off-label by doctors for anxiety symptoms, as SSRIs are a well-established treatment class for anxiety conditions.
Off-label means the drug is being used in a way not specifically approved by the FDA, but supported by clinical evidence.
If you experience anxiety alongside depression, fluoxetine may help both, as fluoxetine is FDA-approved for major depressive disorder and depression and anxiety commonly occur together.
Talk to your doctor about whether fluoxetine is appropriate for your anxiety symptoms.
How long does fluoxetine stay in your system?
Fluoxetine stays in your system longer than most other antidepressants.

After stopping this medicine, Fluoxetine takes approximately 1 to 4 days for Fluoxetine itself to be reduced by half, but fluoxetine also converts in the body to an active metabolite called norfluoxetine, which has a much longer half-life of 4 to 16 days.
This means Fluoxetine and Fluoxetine's active metabolite can remain detectable in your system for up to 5 weeks after your last dose.
This is clinically important for two reasons:

Switching medications: If you are switching from fluoxetine to certain other antidepressants, particularly MAOIs, your doctor will require a washout period of at least 5 weeks to allow fluoxetine to fully clear your system and avoid dangerous drug interactions.

Stopping fluoxetine: The long half-life means withdrawal symptoms are generally milder with Fluoxetine than with shorter-acting antidepressants, as Fluoxetine tapers itself out of your system gradually.
Always talk to your doctor before stopping fluoxetine or switching to another medication.
Q: What does Prozac feel like when Prozac starts working?
A: Most people feel lower levels of anxiety, restlessness and tiredness when Prozac first starts to work.
Your sleep, energy and appetite may improve over the first month and you may have a better focus on daily tasks.
However, a depressed mood can take 6 to 8 weeks to fully respond to treatment.
Q: What drugs can cause serotonin syndrome?
A: Common drug classes that can cause serotonin syndrome include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), and opioids like tramadol.

Q: Prozac vs Zoloft: Understanding the Differences Between Two Popular Antidepressants A: Prozac and Zoloft represent two of the most widely prescribed antidepressant medications in the United States.

Both medications belong to a class of drugs known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), which have revolutionized depression treatment since their introduction in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Q: Is Prozac (fluoxetine) safe for dogs?

A: Studies have shown fluoxetine (Prozac, Reconcile), when prescribed by your veterinarian, is usually a safe and effective medicine for dogs for the treatment of behavioral disorders like separation anxiety.
Fluoxetine is most effective when used in conjunction with a behavior modification plan for your pet.
Do not give your dog Prozac or fluoxetine unless Prozac has been prescribed by your veterinarian.
Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome.
Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Furosemide works by increasing the amount of urine the body makes, which helps reduce swelling and symptoms of fluid retention and helps lower high blood pressure.
Furosemide tablets are sometimes called water pills as they increase how much you urinate.
Furosemide is also known as frusemide in some countries.

Furosemide has been available in the United States since the 1960s and comes as tablets (Lasix), an oral liquid, an intravenous solution, and subcutaneous injections and infusions that can be given at home (Furoscix, Lasix ONYU).
Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
numbness or tingling
headache, dizziness
blurred vision
redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.
Serious furosemide side effects:

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to furosemide (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Furosemide may cause other serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out
ringing in your ears, hearing loss
muscle spasms or contractions
pale skin, easy bruising, unusual bleeding
high blood sugar, with increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, or fruity breath odor
kidney problems, with swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath
signs of liver or pancreas problems, such as loss of appetite, upper stomach pain that may spread to your back, nausea or vomiting, dark urine, or jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes)
signs of an electrolyte imbalance, such as increased thirst or urination, constipation, muscle weakness, leg cramps, numbness or tingling, feeling jittery, or fluttering in your chest.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
You should not use furosemide if you are unable to urinate.
Using more than your recommended dose will not make furosemide more effective.
High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.

Before using furosemide, tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, enlarged prostate, urination problems, cirrhosis or other liver disease, an electrolyte imbalance, high cholesterol, gout, lupus, diabetes, or an allergy to sulfa drugs.
Tell your doctor if you have recently had an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or any type of scan using a radioactive dye that is injected into your veins.
Do not take more of furosemide than is recommended.
If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel fine.
High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Furosemide is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to a profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion.
Careful medical supervision is required, and the dose schedule must be adjusted to the individual patient's needs.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines.
Some drugs should not be used with furosemide.
You should not use furosemide if you are allergic to furosemide or are unable to urinate.
To make sure furosemide is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an electrolyte imbalance (such as low levels of potassium or magnesium in your blood)
enlarged prostate, bladder obstruction, or other urination problems
gout
lupus
diabetes
an allergy to sulfa drugs
kidney disease
cirrhosis or other liver disease.
Tell your doctor if you have an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or any type of scan using a radioactive dye that is injected into a vein.
Contrast dyes and furosemide can harm your kidneys.
Subcutaneous furosemide given at home:
Two brands of furosemide are designed to be given under the skin at home rather than in hospital.
Furoscix is used to treat edema in adults with chronic heart failure or chronic kidney disease, including the nephrotic syndrome, and in children weighing 43 kg (94.7 lb) or more.
Furoscix comes in two forms:
the Furoscix ReadyFlow, a prefilled autoinjector that delivers 80 mg of furosemide in about 10 seconds.
Furoscix can be used in adults and in children weighing 43 kg or more.
the Furoscix On-Body Infusor, a wearable device that delivers 30 mg of furosemide over the first hour and then 12.5 mg per hour for the next 4 hours, giving 80 mg over about 5 hours.
Furoscix can be used in adults and in children weighing 43 kg or more.
Do not use the Furoscix On-Body Infusor if you are allergic to medical adhesives.
The Furoscix ReadyFlow contains benzyl alcohol as a preservative.
Lasix ONYU is a pre-programmed infusor containing furosemide that is FDA-approved for the treatment of edema in adults with chronic heart failure.
Subcutaneous furosemide is not for use in an emergency, and Subcutaneous furosemide is not for long-term use.
Subcutaneous furosemide should be replaced with oral diuretics as soon as practical.
Pregnancy:
It is not known if furosemide will harm an unborn baby.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Breastfeeding:
Furosemide may not be safe to breastfeed while using furosemide.
Ask your doctor about any risk.
Furosemide may slow breast milk production.
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein.
A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription.
Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow.
Do not use liquid if you see particles or if liquid is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks.
Clean it and let it dry.
Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold device there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose.
Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press device firmly into place.
Do not remove and reapply it.
Limit your activity while wearing device and avoid bending as much as you can.
Do not exercise or do anything that might knock device off.
Do not get the infusor wet.
Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing device, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where device is placed.
Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean.
You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose.
If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container.
Do not put autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose.
High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily.
Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well.
High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.
Usual adult dose for edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and chronic renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome):
Oral: initial dose 20 to 80 mg orally once.
Initial dose may be repeated at the same dose or increased by 20 or 40 mg no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose, until the desired diuretic effect has been obtained.
Maintenance dose: administer the dose that provided the desired diuretic effect once or twice a day (for example, at 8 am and 2 pm).
Comments: edema may be most efficiently and safely mobilized by giving this drug on 2 to 4 consecutive days each week.
When doses greater than 80 mg/day are given for prolonged periods, careful clinical observation and laboratory monitoring are particularly advisable.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (ReadyFlow autoinjector):
80 mg of furosemide given subcutaneously in about 10 seconds.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (On-Body Infusor):
30 mg of furosemide over the first hour, then 12.5 mg per hour for the subsequent 4 hours.
This dose is delivered automatically by the On-Body Infusor.
In children weighing at least 43 kg, the device must be applied by a healthcare provider or adult caregiver.
Furoscix is not for chronic use and should be replaced with oral diuretics as soon as practical.
People with significantly reduced kidney function may need additional diuretic therapy, because both Furoscix devices deliver a fixed 80 mg dose.
Usual adult furosemide dose for pulmonary edema:
IV: 40 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.
If a satisfactory response does not occur within one hour, a satisfactory response may be increased to 80 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.
Use: adjunctive therapy in acute pulmonary edema.
IV administration is indicated when a rapid onset of diuresis is desired.
Usual adult furosemide dose for hypertension:
Oral: initial dose 80 mg/day, usually divided into 40 mg orally twice a day.
Use: treatment of hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents.
Usual pediatric furosemide oral dose for edema:
Initial dose: 2 mg/kg orally once.
If the diuretic response to the initial dose is not satisfactory, the diuretic response may be increased by 1 or 2 mg/kg, given no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose.
Doses greater than 6 mg/kg body weight are not recommended.
Maintenance dose: adjust to the minimum effective dose.

Use: treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver and renal disease, including the nephrotic syndrome, especially when an agent with greater diuretic potential is desired.

Gabapentin is a prescription medicine used to treat partial seizures, nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia), and restless legs syndrome (Horizant brand only).
Gabapentin may also be prescribed off-label for other conditions including diabetic nerve pain, anxiety, and fibromyalgia.
Gabapentin is thought to work by calming overactive nerve signals in the brain and nervous system.
Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant and nerve pain medication from the drug class gabapentinoids
Gabapentin brand names are Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant, and Relgaabi, which may not be interchangeable.

Gabapentin is not a federally controlled substance, but some states classify Gabapentin as Schedule V and others require gabapentin prescriptions to be reported to their prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP).
Rules on refills and quantity limits vary by state.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), and swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema).
Side effects often improve as your body adjusts, but do not drive until you know how gabapentin affects you.
Gabapentin is FDA-approved to treat partial onset seizures in patients 3 years and older (used with other seizure medicines) and nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia) in adults.
A related product, gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant), is approved for moderate to severe restless legs syndrome in adults.
The approved uses depend on the specific product, and no single gabapentin product is approved for all of these conditions.
See the table below for a breakdown by brand.
Doctors also prescribe gabapentin off-label for other types of nerve pain, including diabetic nerve pain (diabetic neuropathy), and for anxiety, fibromyalgia, hot flashes, and alcohol withdrawal.
Off-label means that the condition Gabapentin is being prescribed for is not an FDA-approved indication.
Different brands of gabapentin are not interchangeable, and Different brands of gabapentin are FDA-approved for different conditions.
Use only the brand and form of gabapentin your doctor has prescribed.
Check your medicine each time you get a refill to make sure you receive the correct form.
Important: Gralise and Horizant are not substitutes for Neurontin or generic gabapentin, even at the same milligram dose.
The release profile differs, and switching without a prescriber's instruction can significantly change blood levels.

Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system.

Gabapentin does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit.
That same effect helps in different ways depending on what gabapentin is treating:
Epilepsy - dampens the runaway electrical firing that causes seizures.
Postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) - reduces the abnormal pain signals from nerves damaged by shingles.
Restless legs syndrome (gabapentin enacarbil / Horizant) - the exact mechanism is less clear, but the same calming effect on overactive nerves is thought to ease the urge-to-move sensation.
Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller.
Gabapentin works directly on the nerves, which is why Gabapentin helps nerve-related pain and why Gabapentin isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains.
Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.

Gabapentin can cause life-threatening breathing problems (respiratory depression), especially if you already have a breathing disorder (such as COPD), are elderly, or if you use other medicines that can make you drowsy or slow your breathing, such as opioids or CNS depressants.
Seek emergency medical attention if you have very slow breathing.
Suicidal thoughts or behaviors.
Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking and after discontinuing Gabapentin.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Tell your doctor right away if you have any sudden changes in mood or behavior, or thoughts about suicide.
Abrupt or rapid discontinuation.
Seizures may occur if you stop using gabapentin suddenly.
Ask your doctor before stopping Gabapentin.
Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, nausea, pain, and sweating.
Sleepiness, sedation, and dizziness.
Avoid driving or participating in hazardous activities until you know how gabapentin will affect you.
Dizziness or drowsiness can cause falls, accidents, or severe injuries.
Brand substitution.
Brands of gabapentin may not be interchangeable.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
Other common gabapentin side effects may include:
unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
nausea or vomiting
headache
trouble speaking
blurred or double vision
tremor
signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body.
Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking Gabapentin and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol.
A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.
Some side effects are more likely in children taking gabapentin.
Call your doctor if the child has behavior changes, memory problems, trouble concentrating, or is restless, hostile, or aggressive.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
drowsiness, dizziness, or weakness
problems with balance or muscle movement
increased seizures
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Gabapentin can cause weight gain, although Gabapentin is not common.
In clinical trials, a small number of people (roughly 2 in 100) gained weight while taking Gabapentin.
Gabapentin can also cause swelling in the legs, feet, or hands (peripheral edema), which may add to weight changes and becomes more common with age.
You should not take gabapentin if you are allergic to Gabapentin.

breathing problems

a history of alcohol use or drug addiction
a seizure

kidney disease, or if you are on dialysis
Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking seizure medicine.
Children taking gabapentin may have behavior changes.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Your family or caregivers should also watch for sudden changes in your behavior.
Pregnancy:
It is not known if gabapentin will harm an unborn baby.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Do not start or stop seizure medication during pregnancy without your doctor's advice, because having a seizure during pregnancy could harm both mother and baby.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of gabapentin on the baby.
Breastfeeding:
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using gabapentin.
Take gabapentin exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Never take gabapentin in larger amounts, or for longer, than prescribed.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of gabapentin.
Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Neurontin can be taken with or without food.
Gralise should be taken with food, with the evening meal.
Swallow Gralise and Horizant tablets whole.
Do not crush, break, chew, or dissolve them.
If you break a scored Neurontin tablet and take only half, take the other half at your next dose, and use Neurontin tablet within 28 days.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Doses are based on weight in children.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
Do not stop taking gabapentin suddenly.
Stopping suddenly may cause increased seizures or withdrawal symptoms.
Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose, usually gradually over at least a week.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests.
Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using gabapentin.
Your kidney function may need to be checked, and your dose may change based on the results.
Store tablets and capsules at room temperature away from moisture and heat.
Store the liquid medicine in the refrigerator; do not freeze.
Follow all storage instructions provided.

Q: Gabapentin for dogs: uses, dosage and side effects A: Gabapentin is commonly prescribed by veterinarians to treat dogs with chronic pain (such as arthritis, back pain, or nerve pain) or to relieve fear or anxiety associated with stressful events (such as car or plane travel, situations with loud noises [such as fireworks], or visits to the vets or the groomers).
Q: Lyrica vs Gabapentin: What's the difference?

A: Both Lyrica (pregabalin) and gabapentin (Neurontin) are both anticonvulsants and gabapentinoids used to treat nerve pain and seizures, but Both Lyrica (pregabalin) and gabapentin (Neurontin) differ significantly in potency, absorption speed, and regulatory status.

Lyrica is generally more potent, faster-acting (peaks in approximately 1 hour), and is a Schedule V controlled substance, whereas gabapentin peaks in 3 to 4 hours, is less regulated in most states, and is usually cheaper.
Q: How long does gabapentin withdrawal last?

A: Case reports have shown that gabapentin withdrawal often lasts for 5 to 10 days, but some people have taken as long as 18 weeks to completely taper off gabapentin while managing withdrawal symptoms.
The symptoms and how long they last depend on how much of the drug you are taking and for how long you’ve been taking it.
Q: Is gabapentin considered a painkiller?
A: Gabapentin (Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant) is commonly used to treat some types of nerve pain but is classified as an anticonvulsant medicine, not as an opioid or narcotic painkiller.
Gabapentin is used to treat nerve pain that can occur due to an outbreak of shingles, restless legs syndrome (RLS), and some forms of epilepsy.
Q: Is gabapentin safe for cats?
A: Yes, Gabapentin is safe for cats when prescribed by a veterinarian.
This medication is commonly used to treat cat pain, anxiety, and feline hyperesthesia syndrome with minimal side effects.
Mild sedation and drowsiness are the most common reactions, which typically improve with continued use.
Q: Does gabapentin help treat nerve pain?
A: Gabapentin can help relieve nerve pain in some people with postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (diabetic foot pain).
Q: How long does it take gabapentin to work?
A: It can take several weeks for gabapentin to reach its full effect, but this depends on the condition being treated and your individual response to the drug.
Q: Does gabapentin cause weight gain?
A: Gabapentin may cause weight gain, but it is an uncommon side effect.
Studies have shown that a small number of people taking gabapentin weight gain.
People who do gain weight may gain about 5 pounds after 6 weeks of use.
Q: Does gabapentin help you sleep?
A: Gabapentin is a prescription medication that may help you sleep.
That may be why Gabapentin has been prescribed for people with insomnia, even though Gabapentin is not approved for that use.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic, often called a water pill, used to treat high blood pressure and to reduce a build-up of fluid in the body (edema).
Hydrochlorothiazide works by making the kidneys pass more salt and water out of the body, so you urinate more.
Hydrochlorothiazide is often shortened to HCTZ on prescriptions and medical records.
Hydrochlorothiazide is available as a tablet, capsule, and liquid (suspension) taken by mouth and is usually taken once or twice a day.
Hydrochlorothiazide is available as:
oral tablet (12.5 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg)
oral capsule (12.5 mg)
powder for oral suspension (10 mg/mL)
Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) brand names included HydroDIURIL tablets (discontinued), Esidrix (discontinued), and Microzide capsules (discontinued); now generic tablets and capsules are available.
The brand name of hydrochlorothiazide oral suspension is Inzirqo.
Hydrochlorothiazide is also an ingredient in many combination blood pressure medicines, including with losartan, lisinopril, valsartan, and more.
Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
High blood pressure:
HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on HCTZ's own or alongside other blood pressure medicines.
Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.
All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children.
Fluid retention:
Hydrochlorothiazide tablets are used to treat a build-up of fluid (edema) associated with:
congestive heart failure
cirrhosis of the liver
kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure
treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines

The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.
The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups.

Yes, for edema due to various forms of renal dysfunction such as nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis, and chronic renal failure.
| Adults and children
Capsules 12.5 mg | Yes | No | Adults
Oral suspension 10 mg/mL | Yes | Yes, for edema due to congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and renal disease including the nephrotic syndrome in adult and pediatric patients.

Hydrochlorothiazide works by inhibiting the kidneys from reabsorbing sodium and chloride, so more salt and water leave the body in the urine, which helps reduce excess fluid buildup (edema).
Exactly how thiazides lower blood pressure is not fully understood.
The early effect is thought to come from a drop in blood volume.
With longer-term use, blood volume returns towards normal while the blood vessels themselves offer less resistance to blood flow.
Hydrochlorothiazide does not usually change blood pressure that is already normal.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic.
Do not take hydrochlorothiazide if you are unable to pass urine (anuria), or if you are allergic to hydrochlorothiazide or to other sulfonamide-derived medicines (sometimes called sulfa drugs).
Before you start HCTZ, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
kidney disease or reduced kidney function
liver disease, including cirrhosis
diabetes
gout or high uric acid levels
high cholesterol or high triglycerides
high calcium levels or a parathyroid gland disorder
low potassium or low sodium levels
lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
glaucoma
an allergy to sulfa medicines or to penicillin
Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
Hydrochlorothiazide may cause jaundice or bleeding problems in a newborn.
Hydrochlorothiazide can also pass into breast milk and may cause serious side effects in a nursing baby, so you and your doctor should decide whether you will take Hydrochlorothiazide or breastfeed.
Fluid and salt imbalance:
Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood.
Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these and is more likely at higher doses, during rapid fluid loss, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after long-term use..
Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment.
Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance:
dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue
fast heartbeat
passing much less urine than usual
nausea or vomiting
seizures
Kidney and liver problems:
HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body, which can lead to sudden kidney injury.
The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or are already low on fluid.
If you have liver disease, small changes in fluid and salt balance can trigger a serious complication called hepatic coma.
Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and watch for changes in alertness.
Sudden vision changes need urgent care:

Rarely, hydrochlorothiazide causes sudden short-sightedness (acute myopia) and a sharp rise in pressure inside the eye (acute angle-closure glaucoma), usually within hours to weeks of starting the medicine.
Stop taking Hydrochlorothiazide and get medical help immediately if your vision drops suddenly or your eye hurts.
Left untreated, acute angle-closure glaucoma can cause permanent loss of vision.
A history of allergy to sulfa medicines or penicillin may increase the risk.
Blood sugar, cholesterol, uric acid and calcium:
Hydrochlorothiazide can raise blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, uric acid and calcium.
Your diabetes medicine or insulin dose may need adjusting, and diabetes that was previously unnoticed can become apparent during treatment.
The rise in uric acid is related to the dose and can cause gout or make existing gout worse.
Because the medicine also affects calcium, Hydrochlorothiazide is stopped before parathyroid function tests, so tell any doctor arranging tests that you take it.
Your doctor will check these levels from time to time.
Skin cancer risk:
Long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide is linked to a small increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, mainly squamous cell carcinoma.

In a large safety study the increase was about 1 extra case per 16,000 people per year, rising to about 1 extra case per 6,700 people per year among white patients who had taken a total of 50,000 mg or more.
Protect your skin from the sun, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen, avoid sunlamps and tanning beds, and have regular skin checks.
Tell your doctor about any new or changing skin growth, or a sore that does not heal.
Lupus and allergic reactions:
Thiazide diuretics have been reported to worsen lupus or bring it on.
Sensitivity reactions can happen whether or not you have a history of allergies or asthma.
The most noticeable effect of hydrochlorothiazide is passing urine more often, particularly in the first few weeks.
This is how the medicine works rather than a side effect, and side effect usually settles as your body adjusts.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction, such as a spreading red or purple rash with blistering and peeling, or skin that is painful to touch.
Stop taking hydrochlorothiazide and get medical help immediately if you have a sudden change in your vision or pain in your eye.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)
fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores or other signs of infection
unusual bruising or bleeding, or pale skin and unusual tiredness, which can be signs of a blood problem
shortness of breath, wheezing, or a cough with frothy mucus
passing much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs and ankles
light-headedness or fainting, especially when standing up
signs of dehydration or a salt imbalance, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, confusion, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat or unusual weakness
Other side effects:
Other hydrochlorothiazide side effects include:
dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia)
weakness
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite
muscle spasm
increased sensitivity to sunlight, causing sunburn more easily
hair loss or thinning
difficulty getting or keeping an erection
temporary blurred vision, or objects looking yellow-tinged (xanthopsia)
swelling and tenderness of the salivary glands
raised blood sugar, sugar in the urine, or raised uric acid

HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses.
Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium.
Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines.
Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended.
Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses.
Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking treatment every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week.
Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.

The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.

Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day

Shake the bottle well before every dose.
Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe.
Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.

Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose.
Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

Does hydrochlorothiazide cause weight loss?
Hydrochlorothiazide is not a weight loss medicine.
Some people see the number on the scales drop in the first days or weeks of treatment, but this is extra fluid leaving the body rather than any loss of body fat, and fluid levels off.
Do not take hydrochlorothiazide to lose weight.
Can you drink alcohol while taking hydrochlorothiazide?
Alcohol can make the drop in blood pressure that happens when you stand up worse, which may leave you feeling dizzy or faint.
The same applies to barbiturates and opioid pain medicines.
Tell your doctor how much you drink so doctor can advise you.
Does hydrochlorothiazide lower your potassium?
Yes.

Hydrochlorothiazide can lower blood potassium (hypokalemia), and this is more likely at higher doses, when fluid is lost quickly, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after taking the medicine for a long time.
Your doctor will check your potassium with blood tests.
Tell doctor if you have muscle cramps, unusual weakness or tiredness, or an irregular heartbeat.
Should you eat more potassium while taking hydrochlorothiazide?
Only if your doctor tells you to.
Low potassium can sometimes be managed with potassium-rich foods, a potassium supplement, or a different type of diuretic that holds on to potassium.
Do not start any of these yourself, because too much potassium can also be harmful, and some people on hydrochlorothiazide do not need extra potassium at all.
Is hydrochlorothiazide 12.5mg enough?
For many people Hydrochlorothiazide is.
In published trials comparing the two doses, 12.5 mg kept most of the blood pressure reduction seen with 25 mg, and low potassium was consistently less common at 12.5 mg.
Starting at 12.5 mg is recommended for adults over 65.

Maximum dose: 8 tablets/24 hours

Maximum dose: 6 tablets/24 hours

Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours

Comments:
Doses should be individually titrated to provide adequate analgesia while minimizing adverse reactions.
Because of the risks of addiction, abuse, and misuse, the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with individual patient treatment goals should be used.
Monitor patients closely for respiratory depression within the first 24 to 72 hours of initiating therapy and following any increase in dose.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.

Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death.
If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep naloxone with you at all times.
A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up.
Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department.
Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness.
Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL

There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.

Three uses are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.

Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.

Q: How and where should I inject insulin?
A: Injecting insulin is not difficult, but Injecting insulin does take a bit of practice.

There are three main sites where insulin can be injected: the stomach area except for a 2-inch circle around your navel, and the soft part of your waist, but not anywhere near your spine; the top and outer part of your thighs, but not your inner thighs or anywhere close to your knee; the outer back of your upper arm where there is a pocket of fatty tissue.
Q: When is the best time to take Toujeo?
A: Toujeo may be given at any time of the day; however, once you have chosen a time, it is best to inject Toujeo within three hours of that time every day.
If needed, you can change the time you administer Toujeo, just talk to your doctor about this.
Q: How long can Toujeo stay out of the refrigerator?
A: Toujeo can stay out of the refrigerator for up to 56 days (8 weeks) according to the prescribing information written on 03/2023.
If Toujeo if left out the refrigerator for more than 20 or 30 minutes, Toujeo should not be put back into the refrigerator.
Q: What are the different types of insulin?
A: Insulins are usually grouped as fast-acting, intermediate-acting, or long-acting.
Within these groups, Insulins can be further classified as human insulin and human insulin analogs.
An insulin analog is a human insulin that has one or two amino acids changed which affects how quickly insulin analog is absorbed after injection and how fast or slow insulin analog acts.
Insulin analogs are usually given within 15 minutes of a meal or at the same time as food.
Q: Soliqua vs Lantus: What’s the difference between Soliqua?
A: Soliqua is a combination of insulin glargine plus lixisenatide, and Lantus only contains insulin glargine.

Both are once-daily injections that are given under the skin (subcutaneously), but Soliqua can only be used in adults with type 2 diabetes whereas Lantus may be used to treat both type 1 and type 2 diabetes in adults and children over the age of six years.
Both are made by Sanofi-Aventis.
Q: Can Toujeo be given twice a day?
A: Even though Toujeo is usually given once a day, some people may experience better blood sugar control if the dose is split and given twice a day (every 12 hours).
Q: How many pens are in a box of Toujeo?
A: There are three pens in a box of Toujeo Solostar.
There are two pens in a box of Toujeo Max Solostar.
Q: Is Toujeo a fast or long-acting insulin?
A: Toujeo is a long-acting insulin that is usually given once a day.
Toujeo lasts for up to 36 hours.

Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces.
Levothyroxine belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and Levothyroxine works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone).

Levothyroxine replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly.

This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression.
When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although levothyroxine may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet.
Levothyroxine does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid.
Levothyroxine is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to levothyroxine: hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Allergic reactions are usually caused by the inactive ingredients in a product rather than by levothyroxine itself, so your doctor may suggest trying a different brand or form.
Levothyroxine may cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
sudden pain or trouble moving your hip, wrist, or back;
fast or irregular heartbeats, or a pounding heartbeat;
chest pain, pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
wheezing or shortness of breath;
swelling in your legs or ankles, or new or worsening breathlessness when lying down;
fever, swollen glands, itching, joint pain, or not feeling well;
nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
confusion or feeling disoriented;
a seizure; or
high blood sugar - increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, fruity breath odor.
Common levothyroxine side effects may include:
fever, hot flashes, increased sweating, feeling too hot;
tiredness;
skin rash, flushing, hair loss;
chest pain, fast or irregular heartbeats, shortness of breath;
headache, leg cramps, muscle cramps, muscle pain or weakness;
tremors, feeling nervous, anxious, irritable, or emotional, sleep problems (insomnia);
increased or change in appetite;
weight loss or weight gain;
changes in your menstrual periods, or difficulty getting pregnant; or
stomach cramps, vomiting, diarrhea.
Most of these side effects happen when the levothyroxine dose is higher than your body needs, which produces symptoms of an overactive thyroid.
Tell your doctor if you have any of symptoms so your dose can be checked.
Side effects in children:

Children taking levothyroxine may also develop increased pressure around the brain (which can cause headaches, vomiting, or vision changes) or a hip problem called slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which causes hip, groin, or knee pain and limping.
Call your child's doctor about any of these symptoms.

Too much levothyroxine in babies can cause the soft spots on the skull to close too early, and in older children Too much levothyroxine can cause the growth plates to close too early, which may reduce final adult height.
Too little levothyroxine can affect a child's learning and growth.
This is why children need regular blood tests and check-ups.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems.
Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of Levothyroxine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make Levothyroxine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small.
Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development.
Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust dose gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions.
Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.
If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine.
Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.

Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems.
Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures.
This is more likely after menopause.
Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma.
Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.
You should not use levothyroxine if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder.
You should not use certain liquid or injectable forms of levothyroxine if you are allergic to glycerin or edetate disodium.
To make sure Levothyroxine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
a thyroid nodule;
thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland);
heart problems such as a heart attack, stroke, angina, or an irregular heartbeat;
a blood clot or a blood clotting disorder;
diabetes (your diabetes medicine may need to be adjusted);
anemia (low red blood cells);
weak bones (osteoporosis), or low bone mineral density;
problems with your pituitary or adrenal gland;
an allergy to any food or drugs;
recently received radiation therapy with iodine (such as I-131); or
kidney disease.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.

Having hypothyroidism during pregnancy may increase the risk of miscarriage, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, or premature birth, and untreated hypothyroidism can affect the baby's brain development.
The benefit of treating hypothyroidism outweighs these risks, and levothyroxine should not be stopped during pregnancy.
Your dose needs are often higher during pregnancy.

Your doctor will check your thyroid blood tests as soon as your pregnancy is confirmed and at least once in each trimester, and will usually put you back on your pre-pregnancy dose straight after you give birth, with another blood test 4 to 8 weeks later.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding.
Levothyroxine passes into breast milk, but no harmful effects on breastfed babies have been reported.
Treating hypothyroidism properly may also help milk supply if Levothyroxine is low.
Your dose needs may be different while you are nursing.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while using levothyroxine, particularly if your dose is higher than you need.
Talk with your doctor about ways to keep your bones healthy.
Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take levothyroxine before eating food.
Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine:
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
Keep using Oral levothyroxine even if you feel well.
Oral levothyroxine may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
Oral levothyroxine can affect the results of certain medical tests.
Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using Oral levothyroxine.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make Oral levothyroxine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Tablets and capsules:
Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water.
A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly.
Take Oral levothyroxine at the same time each day.
Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of mixture is taken.
Do not save mixture for later use.
Do not mix levothyroxine into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Oral solution (liquid medicine):
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine.
Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast.
Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away.
Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
Store Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids in Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids's original bottle.
Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Intravenous levothyroxine:
Levothyroxine is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring:
Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable.
Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7).
Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change.
Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.

If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, an underactive thyroid may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering.
Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

Q: Does levothyroxine cause weight gain or loss?
A: In most cases, levothyroxine causes some weight loss.
According to the American Thyroid Association, when levothyroxine is started, you may lose up to 10% of your weight.
This weight is mainly water weight, since being hypothyroid makes you retain water.
Q: What can I eat for breakfast after taking levothyroxine?
A: Most foods are considered fine to eat for breakfast as long as foods are eaten 30 to 60 minutes after taking levothyroxine.
Levothyroxine should be taken once a day on an empty stomach in the morning.
Q: Can I take other medications with levothyroxine?
A: Levothyroxine is known to interact with many other medications (called a drug-drug interaction), but there are different kinds of drug-drug interactions.
Some interactions require that drugs not be taken at the same time, while other interactions require more frequent laboratory testing or monitoring of your disease symptoms.
Q: How soon after taking levothyroxine can I take omeprazole?
A: There is a known drug interaction between levothyroxine and omeprazole, but the timing of when you take the two medicines is not relevant.
Omeprazole decreases the absorption of your thyroid medication.
If you need to be on a course of omeprazole while taking levothyroxine, your doctor may order more frequent laboratory testing to confirm you are absorbing enough levothyroxine.
Q: Does levothyroxine cause hair loss?
A: Yes, levothyroxine, the main treatment for a sluggish thyroid gland, may cause hair loss in addition to other side effects.
You may experience partial hair loss in the first few months of treatment, but partial hair loss often resolves and goes back to normal in a short time.
Q: How long after taking levothyroxine can you drink milk?
A: You should avoid drinking milk until at least 4 hours after taking levothyroxine.
Dairy products—including milk, cheese and yogurt—contain high calcium levels, which affect how levothyroxine is absorbed into your body.
Q: How long does levothyroxine stay in your system?
A: Levothyroxine will stay in your system for around 4 to 6 weeks.
Levothyroxine takes longer for people with hypothyroidism to eliminate levothyroxine (closer to 6 weeks) than those with normal thyroid function.
Q: What is the difference between Levoxyl and Synthroid?
A: Levoxyl and Synthroid are brand names for the drug levothyroxine.
Both medications contain the same active ingredient, levothyroxine, but Levoxyl and Synthroid contain different inactive ingredients.
Q: Can you take thyroid supplements with levothyroxine?
A: Taking any other medication or supplement with levothyroxine may cause you to need a higher or lower dose of levothyroxine.
Even supplements like calcium or iron can affect absorption of levothyroxine.

Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity.

Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias.
A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.

A boxed warning is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).

Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because Metformin improves how the body responds to insulin.
PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more.
This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth.

Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.

Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines.

Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

Q: What is metilfenidato used for?

A: Metilfenidato is the Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese translation for methylphenidate which may be used to treat children or adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to help with hyperactivity and impulsive behavior, and allow children or adults to concentrate better.
Metilfenidato may also be used to treat adults with narcolepsy.

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Metoprolol works mainly on the heart, so Metoprolol is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart.
This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure.
Because the heart is doing less work, Metoprolol needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina.
Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why Metoprolol still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate.
Metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate are not interchangeable dose for dose:
Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)
Metoprolol succinate, an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)
Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.
Metoprolol is FDA-approved to treat high blood pressure, angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but the two forms are not approved for the same conditions.

Q: Does metoprolol cause weight gain?
A: Metoprolol is not likely to cause weight gain.
However, weight gain can be a warning sign that heart failure is getting worse.
If you are taking metoprolol for heart failure, tell your doctor right away if you gain weight suddenly.
This weight gain is due to extra fluid in the body that may cause swelling in the feet, ankles, legs and belly.
The fluid builds up because the heart isn’t working as well as heart should.
Q: Does metoprolol lower blood pressure?
A: Yes, metoprolol causes the blood vessels to relax, which helps to lower blood pressure.
If you are prescribed metoprolol for high blood pressure, your doctor may ask you to check your blood pressure regularly at home with an automatic, cuff-style device that goes around your upper arm.
Keeping track of your blood pressure at home is one way to help your doctor know if the prescribed dosage of metoprolol is working for you.
Q: Should I take metoprolol in the morning or at night?
A: When you take metoprolol depends on which salt form is prescribed.
Metoprolol tartrate is usually taken twice daily, so Metoprolol tartrate may be taken in the morning then at night.
Metoprolol succinate is taken once daily, so Metoprolol succinate may be taken either morning or night.
Both forms are usually taken with or immediately after a meal.
Follow your health care provider’s directions for when to take metoprolol.
Q: What is the best time of day to take blood pressure medication?

A: Research has suggested that taking your blood pressure medication at night instead of in the morning can provide better blood pressure control at night without compromising daytime blood pressure control and reduce your overall risk of dying because of cardiovascular disease by 45%.

A: Yes, metoprolol can lower resting heart rate.
Metoprolol is a beta-blocking medication that is used to lower blood pressure, as well as relieve chest pain from angina pectoris.
Q: Metoprolol Succinate vs Tartrate: What's the difference between them?
A: Metoprolol is available as two different salts: metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate.

The main difference between metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate is that metoprolol tartrate is only available as an immediate-release tablet which means it must be taken several times per day, whereas metoprolol succinate is an extended-release tablet that can be taken once a day.

As a result, there are differences in the dosages and indications for both metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate and metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate are not considered interchangeable.

A: Medication-induced hair loss represents a significant concern for patients across multiple therapeutic categories.

Q: What foods should I avoid when taking omeprazole?
A: There are no specific foods that interact with omeprazole, therefore there are no foods that you need to avoid.
Q: Pantoprazole vs. omeprazole: What's the difference between them?
A: Pantoprazole and omeprazole are both proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) that reduce stomach acid and show similar effectiveness for healing acid‑related conditions such as erosive esophagitis.

Pantoprazole and omeprazole's main differences relate to FDA‑approved uses, availability (omeprazole is OTC; pantoprazole is prescription), timing with food, and the option for intravenous (IV) pantoprazole in the hospital setting.
Q: How soon after taking levothyroxine can I take omeprazole?
A: There is a known drug interaction between levothyroxine and omeprazole, but the timing of when you take the two medicines is not relevant.
Omeprazole decreases the absorption of your thyroid medication.
If you need to be on a course of omeprazole while taking levothyroxine, your doctor may order more frequent laboratory testing to confirm you are absorbing enough levothyroxine.
Q: Should I take omeprazole with or without food?
A: Omeprazole is usually best to take Omeprazole 1 hour before meals.
When omeprazole is taken with food, omeprazole reduces the amount of omeprazole that reaches the bloodstream.
Q: Can you take an antacid with omeprazole?
A: You can take an antacid with omeprazole if you are still getting symptoms of indigestion because omeprazole can take several days for omeprazole to start working.
Take omeprazole as directed (usually taken once daily on an empty stomach), and take antacids as needed to relieve indigestion pain after eating.
But tell your doctor if several weeks have gone past and omeprazole does not seem to be working or you are still taking antacids.
Q: Is famotidine safer than omeprazole for heartburn?

A: For most people with mild, occasional heartburn, famotidine is usually the safer first choice because famotidine works quickly, can be taken as needed, and has fewer long‑term safety concerns than omeprazole.

Omeprazole, a stronger acid reducer, may be a better option if you have frequent heartburn two or more days per week or confirmed GERD, but omeprazole is linked with more potential risks when used for many months or at high doses.
Q: Can I take omeprazole in the morning and famotidine at night?
A: Yes, you could take omeprazole in the morning and famotidine at night but there are not many studies investigating this approach.
Preliminary results suggest that taking your medication this way may provide superior control of gastric acid secretion at night without compromising the effectiveness of omeprazole in the morning.
More research is needed.
Q: Is omeprazole (Prilosec) bad for your kidneys?
A: Omeprazole (Prilosec) is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that is used to reduce the amount of acid in your stomach and Omeprazole can be bad for your kidneys.
Omeprazole can cause acute kidney injury and may also worsen the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD).
Q: Does omeprazole cause cancer?
A: Long-term use of proton pump inhibitor (PPI) acid-suppressing agents, such as omeprazole, has been associated with an increased risk of stomach cancer (also called gastric cancer).

This is based on the results of several observational studies and is thought to be because PPIs such as omeprazole are potent gastric acid suppressants that may increase the risk of gastric cancer by causing atrophy (thinning) of the stomach lining, elevating levels of a hormone called gastrin, and an overgrowth of bacteria in the stomach.

Q: How long before a meal should you take ondansetron?

A: If you are taking ondansetron for nausea that occurs with meals, then the standard tablet should be taken half an hour to 1 hour before meals, and the orally disintegrating tablet or oral soluble film can be taken 15 minutes before meals.
However, if you are taking ondansetron for constant, all day nausea then ondansetron should be taken at regular intervals during the day as prescribed, with or without food.
Q: How often can you take ondansetron?

A: You can take ondansetron more frequently initially, for example, if you are taking ondansetron to prevent or treat nausea of vomiting from chemotherapy you can take 4mg then follow up with another 4mg dose at 4 and 8 hours after the first dose.
The following day you should only take ondansetron every 8 hours (3 times a day).
If you continue taking ondansetron more frequently than this you are at higher risk of side effects such as constipation, headache, or heart effects.
Q: Chemo side effects: What should I expect and how to cope?
A: Chemotherapy is a drug treatment used to kill fast-growing cancer cells in your body.

While chemotherapy is an effective treatment for many types of cancer, chemotherapy can also damage healthy cells that divide quickly, such as those in your hair follicles, digestive tract, and bone marrow.
This widespread effect on healthy tissue is what causes the various side effects associated with chemotherapy treatment.
Q: Can you take ondansetron while pregnant?

A: Although ondansetron is not specifically approved by the FDA to treat nausea and vomiting during pregnancy (NVP), its use is common, and approximately 25% of pregnant women are prescribed ondansetron to treat NVP.

Overall, studies show the use of ondansetron appears to be associated with an additional 3 instances of oral cleft defects (such as cleft lip or cleft palate) for every 10,000 women exposed to ondansetron during their first trimester.
There may also be a very slight increased risk of a type of heart defect called a ventricular septal defect, but no apparent increased risk of other birth defects, miscarriage, or fetal death.
Q: How long does ondansetron take to work?

Q: Does ondansetron make you sleepy?

Malaise (generally feeling unwell) and fatigue (tiredness or lack of energy) have also been reported in 13% of patients (vs. 2% placebo) when Ondansetron is used orally for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.
