Q: Do statins cause rhabdomyolysis, and how is rhabdomyolysis treated?
A: Rhabdomyolysis is a rare but serious side effect of statins, a class of cholesterol-lowering medications.
Rhabdomyolysis involves the breakdown of muscle tissue, which releases substances into the bloodstream that can cause kidney damage.
While statins are generally safe, rhabdomyolysis from statins is uncommon and most likely to occur at high doses or when combined with certain other drugs.
Q: When is the best time to take simvastatin?
A: The best time to take simvastatin is in the evening.
This is because your body makes most of its cholesterol at night when you are not eating.

One study that measured people’s total cholesterol and low-density lipoproteins found that concentrations of these two lipids were significantly lower when simvastatin was taken in the evening, than when simvastatin was taken in the morning.
Q: Can I drink grapefruit juice with simvastatin?

A: You should not drink grapefruit juice with simvastatin because simvastatin can significantly increase blood levels of simvastatin and increase the risk of side effects such as liver damage and a condition called rhabdomyolysis, which is the excessive breakdown of muscle tissue.
Occasionally, rhabdomyolysis can cause kidney damage and death.

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism.
Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in.
This is why Spironolactone is called potassium-sparing, and Spironolactone is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.

Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of Spironolactone's side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays.
Spironolactone is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on Spironolactone's own.
High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines.
Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.

Fluid build-up (edema) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone.
Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.
Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths.
Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment.
There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets.
The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between the liquid and the tablets without your doctor changing your dose.
Reported spironolactone side effects:

Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia.
In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it.
The chance goes up on higher doses.
It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and breast growth usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so these effects are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped.
How often most of these effects happen is not known, because these effects come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.
Serious spironolactone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to spironolactone: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:

signs of a high potassium level (hyperkalemia), such as muscle weakness or a heavy feeling in your legs, a slow or uneven heartbeat, numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or lips, nausea, or feeling restless and on edge;
a light-headed feeling like you might pass out, which can be a sign you have low blood pressure (hypotension)
little or no urination, or swelling in your ankles, hands, or feet, which can be signs your kidneys are struggling (worsening renal function);
signs of a low sodium level, such as confusion, severe weakness, muscle pain or cramps, feeling unsteady, or slurred speech;
severe or ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, since losing too much fluid and salt can send your blood pressure and kidney function the wrong way;
a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Spironolactone side effects in men:
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones.
Side effects include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection.
Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Spironolactone side effects in women:
Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause.
Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face.
Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so bleeding can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
Long-term spironolactone side effects:
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel.

Over time spironolactone can push your potassium too high, and spironolactone can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout.
This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver.
No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size.
Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level.
A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and A high potassium level often causes no symptoms until A high potassium level is already high.
Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.

Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because Spironolactone blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.
You should not use spironolactone if you are allergic to spironolactone, or if you have:
a high level of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia);
Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder); or
if you are taking eplerenone.
To make sure spironolactone is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
kidney disease, or reduced kidney function;
liver disease, especially cirrhosis or fluid in the abdomen (ascites);
an electrolyte imbalance, such as a low sodium, magnesium, or calcium level;
dehydration, or any illness causing vomiting or diarrhea;
diabetes, since spironolactone can raise blood sugar;
gout or a high uric acid level; or
prostate cancer treated with abiraterone.
Pregnancy:
Spironolactone blocks the effect of male hormones, and male hormones are needed for a male baby to develop normally.
In animal studies, male offspring exposed in the womb showed feminized development.
The limited information available in humans has not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern remains.
Your doctor will usually avoid spironolactone in pregnancy, or talk through the possible risk to a male baby with you.
Untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry real risks in pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than by stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Spironolactone Spironolactone does not pass into breast milk.
Spironolactone's active breakdown product, canrenone, has been found in breast milk in very small amounts that are not expected to affect a breastfed baby.
No side effects were reported in the one infant studied over a short period, and the long-term picture is not known.
Talk to your doctor so you can weigh this up together.
Children:
Spironolactone has not been shown to be safe and effective in children.
The oral liquid is specifically not recommended for treating high blood pressure in children, because of the hormonal effects of the medicine.
Any use in a child must be decided and monitored by a specialist.
Older adults:
Spironolactone is cleared by the kidneys, and kidney function tends to fall with age.
Older adults are therefore more likely to build up a high potassium level, so kidney function and potassium need monitoring.
Take spironolactone exactly as prescribed.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides.
Take spironolactone the same way each day, either always with food or always without.
Food increases how much spironolactone your body absorbs, roughly doubling spironolactone, so switching back and forth changes how much medicine you actually get.
Shake the oral liquid well before every dose, and measure oral liquid with the marked oral syringe, dosing spoon, or medicine cup that comes with oral liquid, not a kitchen spoon.
Do not switch between tablets and the oral liquid without your doctor changing the dose.
They are not interchangeable, and the liquid gives a higher level of medicine in your blood for the same number of milligrams.
You will need regular blood tests to check your potassium, sodium, kidney function, uric acid, and blood sugar.
Keep these appointments even if you feel completely well.
If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep taking spironolactone even when you feel fine.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.
Tell any doctor or dentist treating you that you take spironolactone, and tell your surgeon before any operation.
Spironolactone can interfere with one type of blood test used to measure digoxin, so mention digoxin if you take digoxin.
Do not share this medicine with anyone else.
Store tablets at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C), and protect them from light.
Store the oral liquid at room temperature and keep oral liquid in a tightly closed bottle.

Is spironolactone a diuretic?
Yes.
Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and Spironolactone belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics.
Spironolactone works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water.
Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in.
It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason spironolactone is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe Spironolactone off-label for hormonal acne in women.
Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but Off-label means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason spironolactone is used this way relates to how spironolactone works.
As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone.
Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it.
Any dose is chosen by the prescriber.

Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because Spironolactone may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking Spironolactone for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.

If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever spironolactone is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and spironolactone is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information.
Spironolactone is a diuretic, so Spironolactone usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame.
Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look.
Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often spironolactone happens is not known.
Spironolactone is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning.
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss.
If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?
It depends what you are taking spironolactone for.

Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so spironolactone starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.
The results you notice take longer.
For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show.
For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give spironolactone a couple of weeks before judging it.
For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?
Spironolactone Spironolactone leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of Spironolactone is gone in that time.
Spironolactone's active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours.
Because of half-lives, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone spironolactone has gone, and it takes a few days for spironolactone to clear fully after you stop.
Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?
No.
Spironolactone is not a blood thinner.
Spironolactone does not affect blood clotting and Spironolactone is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are.
Spironolactone is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly.
Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking Heparin and low molecular weight heparin with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does.
Even so, do not stop Spironolactone without speaking to your doctor.

Stopping Spironolactone can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking Spironolactone for heart failure Spironolactone is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer.
If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?
There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone.
What matters more is that you take Spironolactone at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb.
Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night.
If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest.
Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up.
Alcohol is also a problem in Alcohol's own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease.
Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?
Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy.
Spironolactone blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally.

Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding Spironolactone or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant.
Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone.
The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion.
If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and spironolactone is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?
It depends on the reason you are taking spironolactone.
For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism spironolactone goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure Spironolactone would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further.
For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used.
Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men.
If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting dose yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms.
The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.
This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment.
Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that.
Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

A: Winlevi (clascoterone) and spironolactone are both prescribed to treat acne.
Winlevi is a topical cream, while spironolactone is available in an oral tablet and oral suspension.
Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH.

These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
Tamsulosin works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure, and Tamsulosin is not approved for use in women or children.
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint.
This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start Tamsulosin again after a break.
Get up slowly from sitting or lying down.
Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity.
Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment priapism can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together.
Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery.
Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken tamsulosin in the past, even if you stopped months ago.
Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to.
If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again.
You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin.
Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
To make sure tamsulosin is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an allergy to tamsulosin or any of tamsulosin's ingredients
an allergy to sulfa drugs
kidney problems
liver problems
low blood pressure (hypotension)
Also tell your doctor if you are planning to have cataract or glaucoma surgery.
Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before starting tamsulosin and at regular intervals afterwards.
Tamsulosin is not approved for use in women or in children.
Take tamsulosin exactly as prescribed.
Follow the directions on your prescription label and read any medication guides or instruction sheets.
Take once a day, about 30 minutes after the same meal each day.
For example, 30 minutes after dinner.
Swallow the capsule whole.
Do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, do not start again without talking to your doctor.
Store at room temperature, away from moisture and heat.

Usual adult dose for benign prostatic hyperplasia:
0.4 mg by mouth once a day, taken about half an hour after the same meal each day.
If symptoms have not improved after 2 to 4 weeks at 0.4 mg, the dose may be increased to 0.8 mg once a day.
Tamsulosin 0.4 mg should not be taken with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
If tamsulosin is stopped or interrupted for several days, treatment should start again at 0.4 mg once a day.

What are the common side effects of tamsulosin?
Common tamsulosin side effects may include:
headache
dizziness
runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough, sinus congestion
flu-like symptoms or infection
weakness or lack of energy
back pain, chest pain
diarrhea, nausea
drowsiness or trouble sleeping
tooth problems

reduced interest in sex

Some side effects are more likely at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at the usual 0.4 mg starting dose.

Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition.
Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise.

Mounjaro is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning Tirzepatide activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
Tirzepatide works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
Diarrhea
Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:

Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation.
Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Who should not use tirzepatide:
Type 1 diabetes patients (tirzepatide is not approved for type 1 diabetes)
Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Use with Caution:
History of pancreatitis (safety not established in patients with prior pancreatitis)
Severe gastrointestinal disease
Diabetic retinopathy complications.
Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors.
Possible Thyroid Tumors (Including Cancer):
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer.
In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer.
It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people.

Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Tell your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to tirzepatide, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in tirzepatide.
There is a list of ingredients in tirzepatide, at the bottom of this page.
Tell your healthcare team if you are planning surgery or other procedure that uses anesthesia or deep sedation.
Tell your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney or pancreas disease, a history of diabetic retinopathy or any stomach problems such as difficulty digesting food.
Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding.
If you become pregnant while taking tirzepatide, you should tell your doctor.
There is a pregnancy exposure registry for women who take Zepbound during pregnancy.
Talk to your healthcare provider about how you can take part, call 1-844-524-0039, or visit https://pregnancyregistry.lilly.com/zepbound.

You should follow the directions on your prescription label carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to explain any part you do not understand.
It is important to use this medicine exactly as directed.
Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor.
Tirzepatide is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) using a pre-filled single-dose pen, a multi-dose KwikPen (for single patient use), and a single-dose vial with a syringe.
Caregivers or patients should be trained on proper injection techniques and should read the instructions for use.
Children should not inject Children with the KwikPen; an adult caregiver should give a child a child's injections.
Tirzepatide is usually given:
once a week.
can be given with or without meals at any time of the day.
may be injected into the thigh, abdomen, or have another person inject Tirzepatide into the back of your upper arm
You should rotate injection sites with each dose.
Do not inject into a muscle (intramuscularly) or vein (intravenously).
Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection.
You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking Tirzepatide without talking to your doctor.
Tirzepatide KwikPen:
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until KwikPen stops AND the 1 icon is in the dose window.
After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine.
The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses.
Do not inject the leftover medicine.
Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.
Do not share your tirzepatide Pen with other people, even if the pen needle has been changed.
You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from other people.
People who are blind or have vision problems should not use the Pen without help from a person who has been trained to use the pen.
Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Further dose increases: After at least 4 weeks on the current dose, the dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
If additional glycemic control is needed: Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.
Dose of Mounjaro to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk (Adults With Type 2 Diabetes at High Risk):
The same dosing and escalation schedule applies.
Start at 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week and increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose, up to a maximum of 15 mg once a week.
In the SURPASS-CVOT trial, participants were titrated to 15 mg once weekly or participants's maximum tolerated dose.
How to Use Mounjaro:
Give once weekly at any time of day, with or without meals.
Inject subcutaneously into the abdomen or thigh.
Another person may inject into the back of the upper arm.
Rotate injection sites with each dose.
Missed dose: Give as soon as possible within 4 days (96 hours).
If more than 4 days have passed, skip the missed dose and give the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.
The day of weekly administration can be changed, if necessary, as long as the time between the 2 doses is at least 3 days (72 hours).

Q: Zepbound vs Mounjaro: Comparison Guide for Weight Loss and Diabetes Treatment A: Zepbound and Mounjaro contain tirzepatide and are made by Eli Lilly.
Zepbound and Mounjaro are both administered as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection, but Zepbound and Mounjaro have different FDA-approved indications and insurance coverage.
Q: Which GLP-1 drug is best for weight loss?
A: The most effective GLP-1 drug for weight loss currently (as of early 2026) is tirzepatide, marketed under the names Zepbound (for weight loss) and Mounjaro (for diabetes).
Clinical trials and recent meta-analyses consistently show tirzepatide delivers the most substantial weight reduction among GLP-1 medications, with average losses of up to 22.5% of body weight.
Q: How long does it take for Mounjaro (tirzepatide) to start working?
A: Mounjaro (generic name: tirzepatide) will start to lower your blood sugar levels right away but Mounjaro can take 8 to 12 weeks to reach your target A1C goal.
When compared to some other diabetes treatments, studies have shown that Mounjaro can take 8 weeks to reach an A1C target of ≤7% and 12 weeks to reach an A1C ≤6.5% with Mounjaro.
Significant weight loss can occur as early as 28-weeks.
Q: Tirzepatide vs semaglutide: How do Tirzepatide vs semaglutide compare?
A: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prescription medicines used for type 2 diabetes and long-term weight management.
Semaglutide products include Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy, and Wegovy HD, while tirzepatide products include Mounjaro and Zepbound.
These medicines differ in dosing, approved uses, side effects, and cost, so discuss options with your healthcare provider.
Q: How does retatrutide compare to tirzepatide?

A: Retatrutide is an investigational triple hormone agonist (GLP-1, GIP, glucagon) showing promising early results for obesity and type 2 diabetes, while tirzepatide is an FDA-approved dual agonist (GLP-1, GIP) available for use today.
Q: How much is Zepbound with or without insurance?

Q: Can you get tirzepatide from a compounding pharmacy?
A: Tirzepatide cannot be legally compounded in a U.S. pharmacy at this time because Tirzepatide was removed from the FDA drug shortage list as of October 2, 2024.
When drugs are in short supply, the FDA can allow temporary compounding of some medicines so that patients can access their treatments.
Tirzepatide is now widely available as a prescription medicine made by Eli Lilly under the brands names Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes) and Zepbound (for weight loss and sleep apnea).
Q: How much weight can I lose on Zepbound?

Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period.
An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death.
Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet.
Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available.

Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin?)
Tramadol first gained FDA approval on March 3, 1995.
Originally, tramadol was classified as a non-controlled substance, but tramadol was reclassified in 2014 to Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act with restrictions on tramadol's prescribing.
Tramadol is an opioid (see Is tramadol an opioid?
A person's genetics can affect the pain-relieving properties of tramadol (see How do genetics affect tramadol?
Tramadol is used for the management of moderate to moderately severe pain in adults, including postoperative pain (pain after surgery).
Tramadol treats pain severe enough to require opioids and may be used as an alternative to other forms of pain relief that did not relieve pain well enough or were not tolerated.
Tramadol extended-release capsules may be used by adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their moderate to moderately severe chronic pain for an extended time.

Tramadol should not be used in children younger than 12 years old, or anyone younger than 18 years old with other risk factors (such as breathing problems), or who have recently had surgery to remove their tonsils or adenoids.
Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER) should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Yes, tramadol is an opioid.
The opioid activity of tramadol is due to tramadol's binding to mu-opioid receptors.
Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose).
When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur.
Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.

Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol.
Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol.
You should be given a Medication Guide each time you fill a tramadol prescription.
Read tramadol every time, even if you have taken tramadol before, because the information may have changed.
Your healthcare provider or pharmacist should also go through the risks of tramadol and how to take tramadol safely with you, and explain what to do in an emergency.
Never give anyone else your tramadol.
Anyone else could die from taking tramadol.
Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law.
Store tramadol securely, out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home.
Common side effects:
The most common side effects of tramadol are:
dizziness or vertigo
nausea
constipation
headache
drowsiness
vomiting
itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.
A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?
Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming.
MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription.

Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law.
A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up.
Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.

Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia).

Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol.
Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended.

Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.

You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others).
Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.

Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use tramadol with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily.
If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so healthcare provider can help you find the right treatment and support.
Fatal side effects can occur if you use tramadol with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing.
People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time.
Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death.
People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk.
Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).
Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia.
Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition.
They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6.
People's bodies convert tramadol into tramadol's active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose.
Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids.

Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks.
Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time.
Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating.

Pregnancy:
Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy.
Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated.
Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported.
Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor.
It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks.
If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking tramadol without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both.
Breastfeeding:
Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as tramadol may harm your baby.
Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of tramadol's active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant.
Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness.

If you take the oral solution:
Tramadol oral solution is measured in millilitres (mL), not milligrams (mg), and contains 5 mg of tramadol in every 1 mL.
Confusing the two units can cause a fatal overdose.
Always measure your dose with a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup marked in mL, which your pharmacy can supply, and never with a household teaspoon or tablespoon.

Adult Tramadol Dosage for Pain:
Immediate-release formulations (tablets and oral solution)
Treatment usually starts at 25 mg a day, increasing by 25 mg every 3 days to reach 100 mg a day (25 mg four times a day).
Doses of 25 mg are measured using the oral solution, as immediate-release tramadol tablets are only available as 50 mg.
For the immediate-release tablets, a common starting dose is one 50 mg tablet a day to see how well you tolerate 50 mg tablet, or the dose prescribed by your doctor.
If needed, the total daily dose can then be increased by 50 mg every 3 days as tolerated, to reach 200 mg a day (one 50 mg tablet four times a day).
After this titration, 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) can be taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain.
The maximum is 400 mg a day: eight 50 mg tablets in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution.
Extended-release capsules and tablets
Tramadol ER 100 mg once a day (one 100 mg tablet or capsule) at approximately the same time each day.
Can be increased by 100 mg every 5 days if needed, to a maximum of 300 mg a day, taken as one dose once a day.
Extended-release tramadol is not intended for as-needed pain relief, and should not be taken with any other tramadol product.
Dosage in kidney or liver impairment
Severe kidney impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, doses are spaced 12 hours apart, and the maximum is 200 mg a day (four 50 mg tablets, given as two 100 mg doses 12 hours apart).
Severe liver impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, the recommended dose is 50 mg (one 50 mg tablet) every 12 hours, which is 100 mg a day.
Extended-release tramadol is not recommended for people with severe kidney or severe liver impairment.
Dosage in older adults

No separate maximum dose applies on the basis of age, but tramadol should be started at the low end of the dosing range and increased slowly, with frequent review for drowsiness and breathing problems.
Side effects that led people to stop treatment were more common over the age of 75, mostly stomach and bowel effects, such as constipation.
Kidney function also tends to decline with age, which affects how tramadol is cleared, so your doctor may take this into account when choosing your dose.

Q: Can You Take Tramadol with Acetaminophen, Ibuprofen, or Aspirin?
A: Yes, for most people, tramadol can be safely combined with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin, and doing so can provide better pain relief than either medicine alone.
However, there are important age restrictions and clinical considerations to be aware of.
Q: How much tramadol should I give my dog?
A: How much tramadol you give your dog depends on the size of your dog.
Smaller dogs do not need as much tramadol as larger dogs need to relieve pain.
If you give too much tramadol your dog is likely to have more severe side effects.
The tramadol dosage for dogs is usually between 0.45 to 1.8 mg per pound of body weight (1mg to 4 mg/kg).
The frequency varies depending on what you are giving tramadol for.
For general pain, tramadol is given every 8 to 12 hours, but for cancer-related pain, tramadol can be administered every 6 hours.
Q: How long does it take for tramadol to start working?
A: Tramadol generally starts to relieve pain within an hour in its fast-acting forms, which are used for short-term pain management.
With slow-release or extended-release (ER) forms, Tramadol may take longer to start because it’s gradually released over 12 or 24 hours, but pain relief lasts longer.
Q: How long does tramadol withdrawal last?
A: Symptoms of tramadol withdrawal can start 8-24 hours after the last dose.
Untreated, withdrawal symptoms usually last for 4-10 days.
Withdrawal is caused by stopping tramadol suddenly.
Q: Is tramadol stronger than codeine?
A: Both tramadol and codeine are prescription painkillers used to treat moderate pain, and tramadol and codeine are generally considered comparable in terms of pain relief.
Tramadol is sometimes considered slightly more effective for moderate to moderately severe pain due to Tramadol's dual mechanism of action, but both are classified as "weak" opioids.
Q: How long does tramadol stay in your system?
A: Tramadol is eliminated from your system within roughly 2 days of taking tramadol, but this does not mean that tramadol can no longer be detected by certain drug tests.
Q: Can you take ibuprofen 800 mg with tramadol 50 mg?
A: Yes, you can take these medications together.
Tramadol is safe to take with ibuprofen and may be used to provide additional pain relief.
But be aware 800mg ibuprofen is a high dose of ibuprofen that may cause gastrointestinal side effects such as abdominal pain or reflux if taken long term.
Q: Is tramadol an anti-inflammatory or muscle relaxant?
A: No, Tramadol is not an anti-inflammatory drug or muscle relaxer.
Because it’s not an anti-inflammatory drug, Tramadol likely won’t reduce any swelling you have when taken alone.
Q: Does tramadol raise or lower blood pressure?
A: Tramadol has been linked to both high blood pressure and low blood pressure.
But, neither adverse reaction is common when Tramadol is taken as directed.

A: Trazodone is mostly cleared from a healthy adult’s body within 1 to 3 days after a single dose.
